<meta>continues from previous page</meta>falling short of nine tenths of an inch, reaching only two tenths, or four or five tenths, this constitutes deficiency. When failing to reach a full inch behind the barrier, manifesting at only eight tenths, or five or six tenths, this constitutes deficiency. 

When the primary vessels govern the illness, there is harmony. 

When the illness is contracted within the sinews and bone marrow, and the pulse is intermittent while also surging, the illness is contracted from wine and sexual indulgence. The reason one knows that after five days an ulcerated swelling would form, and after eight days he would vomit pus and die, is that when examining his pulse, the lesser <term>yang</term> <gloss>active, exterior bodily principle</gloss> had begun to alternate. An alternating pulse indicates a disease of the primary vessel. When the illness passes, it moves to the human body; entering the human body, it moves into the collateral vessels governing the illness. At that time, the lesser yang pulse had first reached one tenth of an inch at the barrier position. Therefore, there was internal heat, but the pus had not yet erupted. When it reached five tenths of an inch, it reached the boundary of the lesser yang. 

<note>Collected Explanations: Xu Guang says: 'One' is also written as 'tenth'. The later chapter states that the liver and heart are five tenths of an inch apart, which is why it is said that after five days it is exhausted.</note> <note>Correct Meaning: Wang Shuhe's Pulse Classic states: 'Distinguishing the boundaries of the three gates and what the pulse signs govern: It is said that from the fish border to the high bone, moving backward one inch, the middle is called the cun mouth. From the high bone past the cun to the cubit, it is called the cubit marsh. Therefore it is called cun and cubit. Behind the cubit and in front of the cun is called the barrier. Yang emerges and yin enters, with the barrier serving as the boundary. Yang emerges three tenths of an inch, hence it is called three yin and three yang. Yang is born at the cubit and moves at the cun. Yin is born at the cun and moves at the cubit. The cun governs directing upward to the upper burner, emerging at the head and skin and hair, reaching the hands.'</note>

<summary>This page records Chunyu Yi's diagnostic pulse analysis from the Records of the Grand Historian, explaining how the pulse positions and measurements reveal the progression of internal heat into fatal ulceration, accompanied by commentary on anatomical pulse boundaries from Xu Guang and the Pulse Classic.</summary>
<keywords>Shiji, Chunyu Yi, Wang Shuhe, Xu Guang, pulse diagnosis, lesser yang, barrier pulse, cubit pulse, cun mouth, collateral vessels</keywords>

The <term>liver</term> <gloss>gan</gloss> weighs four catties and four ounces. It has three lobes on the left and four lobes on the right, making seven lobes in total. It governs the storing of the <term>ethereal soul</term> <gloss>hun</gloss>. The liver is a trunk <note>original: "幹", a pun on gan</note>. In the Five Elements, it is Wood, and its physical form has branches and trunks. The spirits of the liver are seven persons. <term>Laozi</term> named their dwelling the Bright Hall Palace, Palace Bureau of the Orchid Terrace <note>original: "明堂宮蘭臺府"</note>, attended by three thousand six hundred subordinate officials. Another source says that the liver spirits are six boys and three girls. 

The <term>heart</term> <gloss>xin</gloss> weighs twelve ounces. Within it are seven pores and three hairs. It contains three tenths of a pint of seminal fluid. It governs the storing of the <term>spirit</term> <gloss>shen</gloss>. The heart is fine and subtle <note>original: "纖", a pun on xin</note>, for what it perceives is subtle and delicate. Its spirit is Nine Grand Commanders <note>original: "九太尉公"</note>, named Grand Origin of the Crimson Palace, Venerable Person of the South Pole <note>original: "絳宮太始南極老人"</note>, possessing a body of circular radiance, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. It is also the sovereign ruler of the body. 

The <term>spleen</term> <gloss>pi</gloss> weighs two catties and three ounces. It is flat and three inches wide, five inches long, and has half a catty of diffuse fatty tissue. It governs the wrapping of blood and warming of the five <term>viscera</term> <gloss>zang</gloss>, and governs the storing of <term>intention</term> <gloss>yi</gloss>. The spleen provides assistance <note>original: "裨", a pun on pi</note>, aiding the vital energy and governing the transformation of grain. Its spirit is called the Jade Maiden Mother of Radiant Cloud <note>original: "雲光玉女子母"</note>, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. 

The <term>lungs</term> <gloss>fei</gloss> weigh three catties and three ounces. They have six lobes and two ears, making eight lobes in total. They govern the storing of the ethereal soul and corporeal soul <note>original: "魂魄"</note>. The lungs mean sudden flourish <note>original: "孛", a pun on fei</note>, meaning that their vital energy flourishes suddenly and is therefore short, being congested. Their spirit is eight persons, the Lords of Great Harmony <note>original: "太和君"</note>, named Jade Hall Palace, Imperial Secretarial Bureau <note>original: "玉堂宮尚書府"</note>, with three thousand six hundred attendant officials. Another source says that the lung spirits are fourteen boys and seven girls. 

The <term>kidneys</term> <gloss>shen</gloss> are two in number, weighing one catty and one ounce. They govern the storing of the <term>will</term> <gloss>zhi</gloss>. The kidneys guide <note>original: "引", an etymological gloss on shen</note>. The kidneys belong to Water, governing the guiding of water vapor to irrigate the various channels. Their spirits are six persons: the Minister of Works, the Minister of Instruction, the Director of Destinies, the Director of Records, the Colonel of Censors, and the Commandant Magistrate <note>original: "司徒、司空、司命、司録、司隸校尉、尉卿"</note>. 

The <term>gallbladder</term> <gloss>dan</gloss> lies between the short lobes of the liver, weighing three ounces and three zhu. It contains three tenths of a pint of seminal fluid. The gallbladder signifies bravery <note>original: "敢", a pun on dan</note>, meaning that a person possesses gallbladder energy and is therefore able to be resolute and courageous. Wu and Jiaoxi are prominent among the feudal lords. Once under scrutiny, neither can hope to remain secure in quiet indulgence. The King of Wu has an internal illness of his own and has been unable to pay court to the Emperor for more than twenty years. He has long worried that he is suspected, and has found no way to clear his name. Even now he draws in his shoulders and treads lightly with overlapping feet in apprehension, fearing he will not be spared. I have also quietly heard that Your Great King has incurred censure over matters of nobility rank."

<note>Correct Meaning: The pronunciation of di <gloss>censure or penalty</gloss> is indicated by the fanqie spelling zhang-ge.</note>

"From what I hear, when feudal lords have their territories stripped, their missteps never warranted such severe measures. I fear this will not stop at the mere confiscation of land!"

The King replied, "Indeed, this has happened. What would you have me do?"

Gao said, "Those who share an enmity assist one another; those who share fond passions keep company together; those who share similar sentiments bring each other success; those who share the same desires run in the same direction; and those who pursue a common benefit will die for each other. Now the King of Wu believes he shares the very same distress as Your Great King. He wishes to adapt to the times, follow reason, and cast aside his own life to rid the world of this looming peril and ruin. Would such an intention be agreeable to you?"

The King was visibly startled and alarmed.

In the court discussion, he said, "Whenever Han has concluded a marriage alliance with the Xiongnu, it rarely lasted more than a few years before they broke the treaty again. It would be better not to grant it, but rather to raise troops and attack them."

Anguo said, "Fighting across a thousand leagues brings no advantage to an army. At present, the Xiongnu rely on the swiftness of their warhorses and harbor the hearts of beasts. Moving like birds taking flight, they are difficult to capture and control. Winning their lands is not enough to expand our territory; taking their populace is not enough to strengthen our state. Since high antiquity, they have never been reckoned as subjects of our civilization <note><term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: Jin Zhuo states that they did not submit internally to Han to become civilized subjects.</note>. If Han marches several thousand leagues to vie for gain, men and horses will be exhausted, while the enemy will use their full strength to exploit our weariness. Furthermore, when an arrow shot from a powerful crossbow reaches the end of its flight, it cannot pierce even thin Lu silk <note><term>Jijie</term> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>: Xu Shen says that the silk of Lu was exceptionally thin.</note>; when a tempest dies down, its final force cannot stir a swan's down. This is not because the shot or the wind lacked vigor at first, but because their strength fades at the end. Launching an attack on them would be unfavorable. It is better to grant the marriage alliance."

Most of the ministers participating in the deliberation agreed with Anguo. Thereupon, the Emperor approved the marriage alliance. In the following year, the first year of the Yuanguang era <note>134 BCE</note>,

<summary>Wang Hui advocates attacking the Xiongnu rather than making another short-lived marriage alliance, but Han Anguo persuades Emperor Wu and the court that distant campaigns against elusive nomads bring exhaustion and defeat. Persuaded by Anguo's famous arguments on military limits, the emperor approves the peace alliance.</summary>
<keywords>Han Anguo, Wang Hui, Xiongnu, marriage alliance, Emperor Wu of Han, Jin Zhuo, Suoyin, Jijie, Yuanguang era, Shiji</keywords>

Tang and Wu had no choice but to ascend the throne. If this was not receiving the Mandate of Heaven, what was it?"

Master Huang replied: "Although a cap may be worn and tattered, it must be placed upon the head. Although shoes may be brand new, they must be fitted upon the feet. Why is this so? It is because of the proper distinction between above and below. Now, although Jie and Zhou departed from the Way, they were nonetheless rulers above. Although Tang and Wu were sages, they were nonetheless subjects below. When a sovereign acts amiss, if his subjects cannot remonstrate with upright words and rectify his errors to honor the Son of Heaven, but instead seize upon his transgressions to execute him and take his place, facing south upon the throne, if that is not regicide, what is it?"

Master Yuangu replied: "If it must be as you say, then when the Founding Emperor <note>Emperor Gaozu of Han</note> replaced the Qin dynasty and assumed the throne of the Son of Heaven, was he in the wrong?"

Thereupon Emperor Jing intervened, saying: "One who eats meat without eating horse liver

When Zhou became <term>Tingwei</term> <gloss>Commandant of Justice</gloss>, imperial trials also multiplied ever more. Those with salaries of two thousand <term>shi</term> <gloss>piculs, ranking high officials</gloss> who were imprisoned succeeded one another continuously, never falling below a hundred persons. Commandery officials and senior provincial headquarters reported cases to the Commandant of Justice.

<gloss>Collected Explanations: Ru Chun states that commandery officials refers to the commandery grand administrators. Meng Kang states that reporting to the Commandant of Justice meant submitting articles of impeachment to the Commandant of Justice for judicial handling.</gloss>

In a single year, these reports reached more than a thousand memorials. In major cases, the persons arrested for confrontation and testimony numbered in the hundreds; in minor cases, several dozen people. The distances involved ranged from several thousand to several hundred <term>li</term> <gloss>Chinese miles</gloss>. When cases were brought to trial, prison officials cross-examined them strictly according to the charges in the impeachment memorials. If the accused did not submit, they were flogged and beaten until their testimony was settled. Thereupon, whenever people heard an arrest was pending, they all fled into hiding. Those held long in prison went through several general amnesties.

<gloss>Collected Explanations: Zhang Yan states that some imperial edicts granting amnesties were not permitted to apply to these orders.</gloss>

For over ten years, the accusations made against one another almost all charged people with the crime of being <term>budao</term> <gloss>devoid of the proper way, heinous treason</gloss> or worse.

<gloss>Seeking the Obscure: We note that "dadi" is like saying "for the most part." "Jindi" means reaching the utmost extremity.</gloss>

Those arrested in the imperial prisons of the Commandant of Justice and the capital magistrates reached sixty to seventy thousand people, and the clerks added more than one hundred thousand more.

<summary>Du Zhou drastically expands judicial purges and harsh interrogations, resulting in tens of thousands of arrests under broad charges of heinous crimes.</summary>

Wuji again slandered Crown Prince Jian day and night to the King, saying: "Ever since Wuji brought in the woman from Qin, the Crown Prince has harbored resentment and cannot help but bear grudges against the King. May the King be somewhat on guard against him. Furthermore, the Crown Prince resides in Chengfu, where he commands troops on his own authority and makes diplomatic ties with feudal lords outside the realm; he intends to enter the capital." 

King Ping summoned the Crown Prince's Grand Tutor, Wu She, and reproached him. Wu She knew it was Wuji's slander, so he said: "Why should the King estrange his own flesh and blood on account of a petty minister?" 

Wuji said: "If you do not control him now, you will regret it later."

Fan Li thereupon departed. From Qi, he sent a letter to Grandee Zhong, which said: "When the soaring birds are gone, the good bow is stowed away; when the cunning hare dies, the hound is boiled.

<gloss><term>Jijie</term> commentary: Xu Guang notes: For <term>jiao</term> <gloss>cunning</gloss>, one source writes <term>jiao</term> <gloss>suburban / open field</gloss>.</gloss>

As for the King of Yue, his character features a long neck and a bird's beak; with such a person, one may share adversity, but one cannot share delight. Why do you not leave?"

Zhong, having read the letter, claimed illness and did not attend court. Someone slandered Zhong, saying he was about to rebel. The King of Yue then bestowed a sword upon Zhong, saying: "You taught me seven strategies for attacking Wu.

<gloss><term>Zhengyi</term> commentary: The <term>Yue Jueshu</term> <gloss>Lost Records of Yue</gloss> states there were nine strategies: First, honor Heaven and serve the spirits. Second, send heavy wealth and silks to present to their lord. Third, purchase grain and straw at high prices to deplete their state. Fourth, send them beautiful women to distract their will. Fifth, send skilled artisans to cause them to erect palaces and high terraces, exhausting their treasury and wearing down their strength. Sixth, flatter their sycophants to make them vulnerable to attack. Seventh, strengthen their forthright ministers so that they are driven to suicide. Eighth, ensure your own state is wealthy and its armaments sharp. Ninth, assemble strong armor and sharp weapons to take advantage of their decline.</gloss>

I used only three of them to defeat Wu, leaving four with you. On my behalf, test them out on our late kings!" Zhong thereupon fell upon his sword and committed suicide. Gou...

<summary>Fan Li flees to Qi and warns Grandee Zhong that Goujian turns upon his ministers in peacetime. Suspected of rebellion, Zhong is ordered by Goujian to commit suicide with a sword, leaving the remaining conquest strategies to be tested in the underworld.</summary>
<keywords>Shiji, Sima Qian, Fan Li, Grandee Zhong, Wen Zhong, Goujian, Yue, Wu, Hegemon, cunning hare, good bow, seven strategies, nine strategies, Yue Jueshu, suicide, Jijie, Zhengyi, Suoyin</keywords>

The realm did not praise Guan Zhong for his worthiness so much as it praised Bao Shu for his ability to recognize worth in others.

<note>Correct Meaning </note><note>original: "Zhengyi"</note>: The Discourses of the States <note>original: "Guoyu"</note> records: Duke Huan of Qi appointed Bao Shu to serve as chancellor. Bao Shu declined, saying: "There are five respects in which your servant does not equal Yiwu: in broad generosity, harmony, and kindness toward the common people, I do not equal him; in governing the state and ruling house without losing hold of the levers of authority, I do not equal him; in loyalty and benevolence capable of binding the common people, I do not equal him; in regulating ritual and duty so they may serve as models for the four quarters, I do not equal him; and in holding the drumsticks and standing at the military gates to inspire the soldiers to greater valor, I do not equal him."

Once Guan Zhong had taken charge of government and served as chancellor of Qi, he used the modest territory of Qi along the coast <note>Correct Meaning: The state of Qi bordered the sea to the east.</note> to circulate commodities, accumulate wealth, enrich the state, strengthen the army, and share likes and dislikes with the common people. For what runs, one may make nets; for what swims, one may make fishing lines; for what flies, one may make tethered arrows. But as for the dragon, I cannot fathom how it ascends into the heavens riding upon the wind and clouds. Today I have seen Laozi: is he not like the dragon?"

Laozi cultivated the Dao and its Virtue. His teachings took self-concealment and being nameless as their primary pursuit. He resided in Zhou for a long time, but seeing the decline of Zhou, he consequently took his leave.

When he reached the frontier pass, Yin Xi, the magistrate of the pass, said: "Master, you are about to withdraw into seclusion. Strive to compose a book for me!"

The <term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure commentary</gloss> cites Li You's <term>Hangu Guan Ming</term> <gloss>Inscription on Hangu Pass</gloss>, which says that Yin Xi detained Laozi and urged him to compose two parts. Moreover, Cui Hao held that Yin Xi was also magistrate of San Pass, which agrees with this.

The <term>Zhengyi</term> <gloss>Correct Meaning commentary</gloss> cites the <term>Baopuzi</term> <gloss>Master Who Embraces Simplicity</gloss>, stating: Laozi traveled west and met Yin Xi, magistrate of the pass, at San Pass. For Xi, he composed the <term>Daodejing</term> in one scroll, entitled <term>Laozi</term>. Others consider it to be Hangu Pass. The <term>Kuodi Zhi</term> <gloss>Comprehensive Gazetteer</gloss> states: San Pass is located fifty-two <term>li</term> southeast of Chencang County in Qi Prefecture. Hangu Pass is located twelve <term>li</term> southwest of Taolin County in Shan Prefecture.

<note>Phonetic commentary: The character <term>qiang</term> <gloss>compel, strive</gloss> has the pronunciation <term>qiang</term> </note><note>original: "其兩反, Fanqie: qi + liang"</note>. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>to Qin. When he arrived in Qin, the King of Qin was delighted with him, but had not yet placed him in a position of trust or service.

Li Si and Yao Jia grew jealous of him and defamed him, saying: "Han Fei is a noble scion of the ducal house of Han. Now, Your Majesty wishes to annex all the feudal lords; Fei will ultimately act for Han and not for Qin. This is simply human nature. If Your Majesty does not employ him, yet detains him for long and eventually allows him to return home, you will be leaving a source of disaster for yourself. It would be better to execute him on the pretext of some legal infraction."

The King of Qin agreed with their view and handed Fei over to the judicial officials for trial. Li Si sent a messenger to deliver poison to Fei, instructing him to commit suicide. Han Fei wished to plead his case directly to the King, but could not obtain an audience. Later, the King of Qin regretted his decision and sent an envoy to pardon him, but Fei had already died.

<note>The <term>Jijie</term> <gloss>Collected Explanations commentary</gloss> notes: Pei Yin observes that the <term>Zhan Guo Ce</term> <gloss>Strategies of the Warring States</gloss> states: The King of Qin enfeoffed Yao Jia with a domain of one thousand households and appointed him Senior Minister. Han Fei spoke ill of him, saying: "Jia is the son of a gatekeeper in Liang. He committed theft in Liang, served as an official in Zhao and was banished from there. Now Your Majesty takes the son of a hereditary gatekeeper, a major thief of Liang, and a banished official of Zhao, and joins with him to plan state affairs for the altars of soil and grain. This is not the way to encourage the multitude of ministers." The King summoned Jia and questioned him about this. Jia replied in defense, after which Han Fei was put to death.</note>

Shenzi and Master Han both composed books that were transmitted to later generations, and many scholars possess them. I alone grieve for Master Han, who wrote <term>Shuo Nan</term> <gloss>Difficulties of Persuasion</gloss> and yet could not

<summary>Li Si and Yao Jia slander Han Fei out of jealousy, leading the King of Qin to imprison him and Li Si to force his suicide by poison. Sima Qian cites the commentary regarding Yao Jia's rivalry and begins his personal reflection on the tragedy of Han Fei's fate.</summary>
<keywords>Han Fei, Li Si, Yao Jia, King of Qin, execution, poison, Zhan Guo Ce, Shen Buhai, Difficulties of Persuasion, Shiji</keywords>

exhaustively expresses the adjustments of ritual in order to conclude the discourse of the Book of Ritual.

Establishing exaltation as the ultimate peak, no one in the world can add to or subtract from it. The root and branch accord with each other.

<term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: This means that when ritual is at its flourishing height, cultural patterns and principle unite to return to the Great Oneness. When ritual is reduced, it returns to natural feelings to return to the Great Oneness. That both exaltation and reduction return to the Great Oneness is what is meant by "the root and branch accord with each other."

Beginning and end correspond to each other.

<term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: Ritual begins in simplicity and ends in ease. Ease also means reduction. That reduction and simplicity correspond is what is meant by "beginning and end correspond to each other."
<term>Zhengyi</term> <gloss>Correct Meaning</gloss>: The character <term>ying</term> <gloss>correspond</gloss> is pronounced with the sound of <term>yi</term> and <term>ling</term> combined <note>fanqie phonological spelling</note>, meaning to match or be fitting.

In its utmost cultural refinement, it possesses the means to make distinctions.

<term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: This means that the utmost cultural refinement of ritual can distinguish between the honored and the humble, the noble and the base, which is why it is said to have "the means to make distinctions."

In its utmost discernment, it possesses the means to bring joy.

<term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Seeking the Obscure</gloss>: This means that the utmost discernment of ritual has the means to clarify exaltation and reduction, addition and subtraction, and intricate expressions of emotion and cultural form, which suffice to bring joy to the human heart. Therefore it is said to have "the means to bring joy."

Those in the world who follow it enjoy order; those who do not follow it suffer chaos. Those who follow it find security; those who do not follow it face peril. The petty person cannot take it as a model.

<term>Zhengyi</term> <gloss>Correct Meaning</gloss>: "Petty person" is equivalent to "common person." To "take as a model" means to follow as a standard. This means that from scholars on up to emperors and kings, those who can follow ritual attain good order and peace, while those who cannot follow ritual face danger and disorder. Common people are bound by practical tasks and cannot take ritual as their model.

The outward manifestation of ritual is truly profound. Even the keen discernment of "hard and white" and "sameness and difference" <note>famous philosophical paradoxes of the School of Names</note> enters into it and

<summary>This passage expounds Xunzi's theory of ritual as recorded in the Shiji, explaining how ritual harmonizes root and branch, beginnings and endings, and distinctions of rank with human joy. It emphasizes that adherence to ritual brings social order and security, whereas common folk remain constrained by daily toil and cannot fully model it.</summary>
<keywords>Shiji, Sima Qian, Xunzi, Book of Ritual, Suoyin, Zhengyi, Great Oneness, social order, hard and white, School of Names</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>The principle of great music accords with the <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term> and the pitch pipes, giving birth to and nourishing the ten thousand things: this is how great music shares harmony with Heaven and Earth.

Great rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: This means according with the vital breath of Heaven and Earth and their numerical measures.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: This means that Heaven has the sun and moon, and Earth has mountains and rivers. High and low have distinct forms, and their generative functions are each different. Great rites distinguish nobility and baseness, honor and humility, marking their gradations and differences: this is how great rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth.</margin>

Because of harmony, the hundred things do not lose their course.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: They do not lose their innate nature.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Music shares harmony with Heaven and Earth, and is able to generate and fulfill the innate nature of the ten thousand things.</margin>

Because of moderation, sacrifices are offered to Heaven and Earth.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: For their merit in completing things, recompense is offered to them.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: Rites share moderation with Heaven and Earth. With nobility and baseness, superior and inferior clearly ordered, one offers recompense for the merit of generating and completing the ten thousand things.</margin>

In the manifest realm, there are rites and music.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: These are what teach people.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: "Manifest" is like "external". It means that the sage king can cause music to harmonize with Heaven and Earth, and rites to share moderation with Heaven and Earth, and can make these rites and music luminous to instruct the people.</margin>

In the hidden realm, there are ghosts and spirits.

<margin><term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Jijie commentary</gloss>: Zheng Xuan says: They assist Heaven and Earth in completing things. The Book of Changes says: "One understands the conditions and circumstances of ghosts and spirits." In that case, the refined vital breath of a sage is called a spirit, and the refined vital breath of a worthy or wise person is called a ghost.</margin>

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>: "Hidden" means internal. It means that the sage king can inwardly revere ghosts and spirits, assisting Heaven and Earth to generate and complete the ten thousand things.</margin>

When matters are like this, within the Four Seas, all join in reverence and unite in love.

<margin><term>Correct Meaning</term> <gloss>Zhengyi commentary</gloss>:</margin>

<summary>This passage expounds on the cosmological foundations of music and rites, showing how great music accords with cosmic harmony to nourish all creatures, while great rites mirror cosmic distinctions and moderation. It explains the dual operation of rites and music in the visible realm to educate humankind, alongside reverence for spirits in the hidden realm, thereby cultivating universal respect and love across the empire.</summary>
<keywords>Treatise on Music, Records of the Grand Historian, Sima Qian, rites and music, yin and yang, pitch pipes, cosmic harmony, moderation, sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, ghosts and spirits, Zheng Xuan, Jijie commentary, Zhengyi commentary</keywords>

Feudal lords and nobility bowed their heads and depended entirely upon them for supplies <note>Collected Explanations: Jin Zhuo says: "Di <gloss>低</gloss> is pronounced like di <gloss>抵</gloss>, meaning to resist or oppose." Fu Qian says: "They relied upon the merchants for financial supplies." Seeking the Obscure: Fu Qian's explanation is correct. Liu Bozhuang believed that the feudal lords and great merchants all bowed their heads and pursued private profit to provide for themselves rather than assisting the Son of Heaven, which is incorrect.</note>. Those engaged in metallurgy, casting, and boiling seawater for salt amassed fortunes sometimes totaling tens of thousands of catties of gold, yet they did nothing to alleviate the nation's emergencies, leaving the common people in dire distress. 

Thereupon, the Son of Heaven discussed with the high ministers and court officials the reform of coinage and the minting of new currency to satisfy state expenditures and to crush those opportunistic, extravagant speculators and monopolists. At that time, the imperial park possessed white deer, and the Privy Purse had an abundance of silver and tin.

Since Emperor Xiaowen reformed the coinage to mint the four-zhu coin, more than forty years had passed by this year. From the Jianyuan era onward, because state funds were deficient, the imperial authorities frequently cast coins wherever copper mountains were plentiful. The common people also illicitly minted coins in numbers beyond count. Coins became increasingly abundant and light <note>Collected Explanations: Ru Chun says: "People filed the coins to extract copper for melting down, which caused the lightness." Zan says: "Because those minting coins were so numerous, the value of the coins became light, and being light also made them cheap."</note>, while commodities became increasingly scarce and expensive <note>Collected Explanations: Ru Chun says: "People only manufactured coins and did not produce other goods."</note>. <summary>Wealthy merchants and industrialists amassed vast fortunes through salt and iron while neglecting state crises, prompting Emperor Wu and his ministers to overhaul the currency system. The following year, the Son of Heaven began his imperial tour of the commanderies and feudal kingdoms. Heading east, he crossed the Yellow River. The Administrator of Hedong did not anticipate the arrival of the imperial procession and was unable to supply provisions; he committed suicide. The procession traveled west and crossed the Long Mountains. The Administrator of Longxi, because the imperial procession had arrived suddenly,

<note>Collected Explanations: Pei Yin notes: The Phonetic Meaning of the Han Shu says: "<term>Yu</term> <gloss>to cross</gloss> means to pass over. <term>Zu</term> <gloss>sudden</gloss> means abrupt and unexpected."</note>

could not provide food for the Son of Heaven's retinue; the Administrator of Longxi committed suicide.

Thereupon, His Majesty traveled north through Xiao Pass. Leading tens of thousands of cavalry, he hunted across the region of Xinqinzhong in order to inspect and train the frontier troops, and then returned. In Xinqinzhong, there were areas of perhaps a thousand <term>li</term> without watchtowers or border patrols.

<note>Collected Explanations: Ru Chun says: "<term>Jiao</term> <gloss>border patrol</gloss> also refers to the class of soldiers who pursue thieves." Jin Zhuo says: "<term>Jiao</term> means border barricades or fortifications." Chen Zan says: "There were neither signal towers nor patrolling border guards; there was no defense prepared for guarding the frontier."</note>

Thereupon, the Grand Administrator of Beidi and those beneath him were executed. The common people were then permitted to graze and breed livestock in the border counties.

<note>Collected Explanations: Pei Yin notes: The Phonetic Meaning of the Han Shu says: "This ordered that the people be allowed to raise livestock in the border counties." Once watchtowers and border patrols were established, the people were able to keep livestock."</note>

The government lent them breeding mares, to be returned after three years along with one tenth of the offspring as interest. In this way, the proceeds seized through the denunciation of concealed wealth <note>the <term>gaomin</term> system</note> were used to fill and enrich Xinqinzhong.

<summary>Emperor Wu toured the empire and inspected the northern frontier at Xinqinzhong, punishing regional officials whose negligence left troops unsupplied or borders undefended. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>edition, it is also fitting that they be arranged side by side to engrave the Twenty-Two Histories to match the Thirteen Classics. Receiving the imperial decree, we hurried forward like mallards skimming the water; joining the distinguished ranks of the court, we rejoiced like leaping sparrows. Fine editions have been bestowed from the imperial library <note>original: "秘閣" (*Mi Ge*)</note>, where jade-like volumes assemble in profusion; our duty offices stand close to the forbidden palace grounds, adjacent to the crystalline halls of the celestial realm <note>original: "蕊珠之館" (*Ruizhu zhi Guan*), poetically evoking the imperial library pavilions</note>. Burning the midnight oil, the evening collation continues as the moon already peeks through the blinds; grinding ink for early-morning writing, the dawn breeze turns the manuscript leaves. Rejoicing in this grand occasion of the literary world, we completely forget the toil of our usual labors. Yet the critical verification of these various histories presents difficulties far more intense than comparing variations among the Confucian Classics. The concluding records of an earlier history form the very starting point of the subsequent history; the intertwined events of the southern dynasties are likewise stitched together in the northern histories. As each author wrote according to their own perspective, divergences naturally arose, producing confusion and error. How could there be no sound reading among them? Yet extracting excerpts easily breeds tedious redundancy.

Memorial of Presentation <note>original: "進表" (*Jin Biao*)</note>
Page three

<summary>This memorial recounts the imperial commission to compile and engrave the Twenty-Two Histories alongside the Thirteen Classics, describing the scholars' nighttime labor with palace manuscripts and the historiographical challenges of reconciling divergent and overlapping dynastic accounts.</summary>
<keywords>Twenty-Two Histories, Thirteen Classics, Siku Quanshu, imperial library, text collation, historiography, southern and northern dynasties, presentation memorial</keywords>

In ancient times, the lineage of Dihong had an unworthy son,

<note>Correct Meaning: "Te" </note><note>original: "慝"</note> means evil. Another edition states: "The people of all under Heaven called him Hundun." Hundun was Huandou. This means he suppressed righteous deeds, secretly worked harm, and delighted in vicious malice, which is why he was called Hundun. Du Yu says that Hundun describes an appearance of being closed and unenlightened. The Classic of Divine Marvels <note>original: "神異經"</note> states: "West of the Kunlun mountains there is a beast. Its form resembles a dog with long fur and four feet like a brown bear but without claws. It has eyes but cannot see, and its steps do not advance. It has two ears but cannot hear, yet it senses when human beings pass. It has a belly without five internal organs, and its neck is straight and short so food passes straight through. When it encounters someone of virtuous conduct, it charges and butts them. When it encounters someone who acts with malice and wickedness, it leans upon and relies on them. Its name is Hundun." Furthermore, Zhuangzi says: "The Emperor of the Southern Sea was Shu <gloss>Brief</gloss>, the Emperor of the Northern Sea was Hu <gloss>Sudden</gloss>, and the Emperor of the Center was Hundun <gloss>Chaos</gloss>. Liu Ban remarked: "In my opinion, halting the Yellow River breach and erecting the Longyuan Palace were two distinct events; the construction of the palace was not undertaken simply on account of repairing the river breach. Yan Shigu suspected that it ought to say Longyuan Shrine; yet according to the Annals of Emperor Jing, when the Deyang Shrine was established, it was also referred to as the Deyang Palace. In the fourth year, in winter, Dou Ying, the Marquis of Weiqi, was found guilty of a crime and executed in the public marketplace.

<note>Yan Shigu noted: "This was because he had formed a faction with Guan Fu."</note>

In spring, in the third month, on the day <term>yimao</term> <gloss>day 52 of the sexagenary cycle</gloss>, Chancellor Tian Fen died. In summer, in the fourth month, frost fell and killed the grasses. In the fifth month, an earthquake occurred. An amnesty was granted to all under Heaven.

In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month, Liu De, King of Hejian, died. In summer, troops were dispatched from Ba and Shu to construct the road to the Southern Barbarians. In addition, ten thousand soldiers were mobilized to fortify and open the strategic defiles of Yanmen.

<note>Yan Shigu noted: "This was done to strengthen defenses in order to halt the incursions of the Xiongnu." Liu Ban remarked: "In my opinion, repairing the strategic defiles meant opening the roads to make them level and easy to traverse, solely to facilitate launching campaigns against the Xiongnu."</note>

In autumn, in the seventh month, a great gale uprooted trees. On the day <term>yisi</term> <gloss>day 42 of the sexagenary cycle</gloss>, Empress Chen was deposed, and those who practiced witchcraft were arrested.

<summary>Yan Shigu and Liu Ban comment on the location of Longyuan Palace, after which Dou Ying is executed, Chancellor Tian Fen dies, King Liu De passes away, military roads and passes are fortified against the Xiongnu, and Empress Chen is deposed amid witchcraft investigations.</summary>

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "The character for rain or hail falling <term>yu</term> is pronounced with the fanqie phonetic of yu and ju inverted."</note>

More than ten commanderies and kingdoms east of Hangu Pass suffered famine, and people ate one another. Shun, King of Changshan, died; his son Dun succeeded to the throne, but committed a crime, was deposed, and was banished to Fangling.

In the fourth year <note>113 BCE</note>, in winter, in the tenth month, the Emperor traveled to Yong to sacrifice at the Five Altars. He bestowed one rank of nobility upon each male head of household, and one hundred families of women were granted an ox and wine. He proceeded from Xiayang, traveling east to visit Fenyin.

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "Xiayang is a county of Fengyi. Fenyin belongs to Hedong. The character Fen is pronounced with the fanqie phonetic of fu and yun inverted."</note>

In the eleventh month, on the day <term>jiazi</term>, an altar to the <term>Houtu</term> <gloss>Earth Goddess</gloss> was established on the bank of the Fen River at <term>Chui</term>.

<note>Su Lin stated: "The character Chui is pronounced shui."</note>

<note>Ru Chun stated: "Chui refers to a mound rising abruptly on the east bank of the Yellow River, four or five li long, over two li wide, and more than a hundred feet high. The county seat of Fenyin was governed atop the Chui mound. The altar to Houtu lies west of the county. The Fen River lies north of the Chui mound and flows west to merge with the Yellow River."</note>

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "Both explanations are correct. Chui takes its name from its high, bulging shape resembling a person's buttocks and rump. Another explanation is that this place overlooked the Fen River and was originally named Lin, which sounds the same as kui. The local people pronounced kui like shui, which caused the name to shift."</note>

<summary>This page records portents and natural disasters including a fire at Yangling and severe famine east of the pass leading to cannibalism, followed by Emperor Wu's imperial tour to Yong, his sacrifices at the Five Altars, and the establishment of the imperial altar to the Earth Goddess Houtu at Chui in Fenyin.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>He then dispatched an envoy to persuade him. The Chanyu's envoy arrived but died at the capital. The Xiongnu raided the border, so General Who Plucks the Hu Guo Chang was dispatched to garrison Shuofang.

In the winter of the fifth year <note>106 BCE</note>, the Emperor embarked on an inspection tour southward, arriving at Shengtang.

<note>Wen Ying stated: "According to the 'Treatise on Geography,' there is no such county name. I suspect it should be located near Lujiang." Wei Zhao stated: "It is located in Nanjun." Yan Shigu stated: "Wei's explanation is correct."</note>

From afar, he offered sacrifice to Shun of Yu at Mount Jiuyi.

<note>Ying Shao stated: "Shun was buried at Cangwu. Jiuyi is the name of a mountain, now located in Yingdao of Lingling." Wen Ying stated: "Mount Jiuyi lies half in Cangwu and half in Lingling." Ru Chun stated: "Shun was buried at Jiuyi, and Jiuyi is located in Fengcheng County of Cangwu; hence it is sometimes said that Shun was buried at Cangwu." Yan Shigu stated: "Wen's explanation is correct. The character <term>yi</term> <gloss>嶷</gloss> is pronounced like <term>yi</term> <gloss>疑, doubt</gloss>. The mountain has nine peaks whose forms and appearances closely resemble one another, which is why it is called Mount Jiuyi <gloss>Nine Doubts Mountain</gloss>." Song Qi stated: "In old editions, after 'is correct' there was the character 'Nine,' and beneath 'yi' there was no pronunciation gloss for 'yi.' The text was corrected according to the Imperial History Office edition."</note>

He climbed Mount Tianzhu in Qian.

<note>Ying Shao stated: "The character <term>qian</term> <gloss>灊</gloss> is pronounced like <term>qian</term> <gloss>潛, submerged</gloss>. Mount Huo, the Southern Sacred Peak, is located in Qian. The character <term>qian</term> is pronounced <term>cen</term>." Yan Shigu stated: "The character <term>qian</term> is pronounced the same as <term>qian</term> <gloss>潛</gloss>. Ying's explanation is correct."</note>

From Xunyang, he floated down the Yangtze River and shot a river dragon with his own hands in the midst of the river, capturing it.

<summary>Emperor Wu dispatches Guo Chang to defend Shuofang against Xiongnu incursions, conducts an imperial progress southward to Shengtang, performs distant sacrifices to Emperor Shun at Mount Jiuyi, ascends Mount Tianzhu in Qian, and personally hunts a river dragon while sailing on the Yangtze River from Xunyang.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>When the Emperor heard of it, he took pity on him, established Luan as King of Sishui, and had the Chancellor and Senior Scribe cast into prison. In the third month, silk fabric was bestowed upon those selected by the commanderies and kingdoms for conduct and righteousness, including Han Fu of Zhuo Commandery and four others, fifty bolts per person, and they were sent home. An edict declared: "We regret to wear them out with the burdens of official duties."

<note>Deng Zhan states: "The Emperor took pity and felt grief for Han Fu and the others, and could not bear to wear them out with labor and service in official duties."</note>

"Let them devote themselves to cultivating filial piety and brotherly respect in order to instruct their local communities. Let the commanderies and counties regularly grant them sheep and wine in the first month. If any among them meets with misfortune, grant them a single suit of clothing and quilts, and sacrifice to them with a <term>zhonglao</term> <gloss>secondary sacrificial offering of sheep and pig</gloss>."

<note>Yan Shigu states: "Fortunate means auspicious and avoiding misfortune; hence death is referred to as misfortune. A suit refers to a complete set, like saying a pair or set today. The <term>zhonglao</term> is the lesser offering <term>shaolao</term>, referring to a sheep and a pig."</note>

The Di people of Wudu rebelled.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The character <term>Di</term> has the fanqie pronunciation of <term>ding</term> and <term>xi</term>."</note>

The Commander of the Capital Gendarmes <term>Zhi Jinwu</term> Ma Shi Jian and Marquis of Long'e Han Zeng were dispatched.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The surname was Mashi and the personal name was Jian. For Long'e, editions of the Hanshu sometimes write the character <term>Luo</term>. The Table of Meritorious Officials and Marquises states that Han Tuodang, Marquis Zhuang of Gonggao, had a son named Gui who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Longluo. In the fifth year of the Yuanding era he was stripped of rank due to the gold offering offense. In the first year of the Houyuan era, Gui's younger brother's son Zeng succeeded to the enfeoffment as Marquis of Longluo. Xun Yue's Han Annals uses the character <term>E</term> for all instances of Longluo. Cui Hao says that <term>luo</term> is pronounced like <term>luo</term>."</note>

Compared to Hu Jian's actions, what doubt could there be?"</note>

From this, Hu Jian became famous. Later, he served as Magistrate of Weicheng <note>original: "渭城令"</note>, where his governance earned great renown. It happened that Emperor Zhao was young, and General Shangguan An, father of the Empress, was on friendly terms with Ding Wairen, the paramour of the Emperor's elder sister, the Eldest Princess Gai. Ding Wairen was arrogant and unrestrained; bearing a grudge against Fan Fu, the former Intendant of the Capital, he sent a retainer to shoot and kill him. The retainer hid in the residence of the Princess, and the magistrates dared not arrest him. Hu Jian, Magistrate of Weicheng, led officers and soldiers to surround and arrest him. When Princess Gai heard of it, she, Ding Wairen, and General Shangguan went with a large entourage of slaves and retainers, rushing on horseback and shooting at the pursuing officers. <note>Yan Shigu states: "*Ben* </note><note>original: '犇'</note> is an ancient form of *ben* <note>original: '奔'</note>, meaning running forward in haste to shoot."

The officers scattered and fled. Princess Gai sent an archer-attendant to indict the Weicheng patrol officer for injuring slaves of the Princess's household. Hu Jian reported that there was no other crime committed. <note>Fu Qian states: "This means the patrol officer was performing public duty and had committed no other crime." Liu Ban states: "The character *ling* <gloss>magistrate</gloss> is superfluous here."</note>

Princess Gai was enraged and sent someone to submit a memorial to the throne, accusing Hu Jian of insulting the Eldest Princess and shooting at <unclear>次字曰字十八字</unclear>

In the way of loving relatives, preserving them whole is foremost. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "Striving to preserve them in security and peace is the highest priority."</note> One ought to grant them worthy teachers and good tutors to instruct them in the way of loyalty and filial piety. Yet now they are honored and doted upon in high positions, and entrusted with supreme authority <note>Yan Shigu comments: "This uses the Big Dipper constellation as an analogy: the body of the Dipper is the bowl, while the handle controls direction. Giving them the handle means granting executive power."</note>, causing them to become arrogant and rebellious until they are exterminated. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "'Yi' means to level, referring to wiping them out completely."</note> This is the greatest failure in loving relatives. Even a man of Huo Guang's worthiness could not plan for his descendants; therefore, when powerful ministers pass authority to the next generation, danger inevitably follows.

The Classic of History says: "Do not let it be like a fire that starts small and faint." <note>Yan Shigu comments: "These are words from the 'Luo Announcement' <term>Luo gao</term> in the Book of Zhou <term>Zhou shu</term>. 'Yongyong' describes something minute and faint. It means that if a fire begins small and is not extinguished early, it will blaze up fiercely. When high ministers monopolize power, one must likewise plan early to strip them of their authority."</note> When their power overawes the sovereign and their authority surpasses that of the ruler, attempting to prevent disaster afterward will be too late. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "'Yi' is a final particle marking the conclusion of the statement."</note>

In that month, Huo Guang's brother-in-law, Palace Attendant and Grand Palace Grandee Zhang Shuo, was also sent out to serve as Grand Administrator of Shu Commandery. His granddaughter's husband, General of the Household Wang Han, was appointed Grand Administrator of Wuwei. Soon after, he again reassigned Huo Guang's eldest daughter's husband, Commandant of the Guards of the Changle Palace Deng Guanghan, to serve as Privy Purse. 

He further appointed Huo Yu as Commander-in-Chief, wearing a small cap without seal and ribbons, and dismissed his right-flank garrison command and subordinate officials. The purpose of giving Huo Yu the official title of Commander-in-Chief alongside Huo Guang was specifically to disarm his authority.

<gloss>Su Lin says: "<term>Te</term> <gloss>specifically</gloss> means merely." Song Qi says: "Regarding the phrase 'making Yu's official title' <note>original: "使禹官名字"</note>, the character <term>guan</term> <gloss>office</gloss> should be deleted, and below the word <term>ming</term> <gloss>name</gloss> the character <term>wei</term> <gloss>to serve as</gloss> should be added."</gloss>

He also seized the seal and ribbon of General of Du Liao from Fan Mingyou, keeping him merely as Superintendent of the Imperial Household. Furthermore, Huo Guang's second daughter's husband, Zhao Ping, who held the titles of Cavalier Attendant, Commandant of Cavalry, and Grand Palace Grandee commanding garrison troops, had his seal and ribbon as Commandant of Cavalry confiscated.

The Appraisement states:
Huo Guang, from the time he bound his hair <note>that is, from his coming of age</note>, served within the inner palace, rising from between the steps and private entry doors. Steadfastly he held to his resolve, and his rectitude was made manifest to the Sovereign
<gloss>Shigu says: "'Manifest' <note>形 <term>xing</term></note> means displayed to sight."</gloss>.
He received the charge over the infant in swaddling clothes <note>Emperor Zhao</note>, and bore the sacred trust of the Han ruling house. Taking charge at the ancestral court, he sheltered and protected the child sovereign; he crushed the King of Yan and struck down the House of Shangguan
<gloss>Shigu says: "'Struck down' <note>仆 <term>pu</term></note> means to overturn or bring down; it is pronounced <term>fu</term>."</gloss>.
Relying upon his authority to subdue enemies, he brought his loyalty to full fruition. Positioned in the midst of depositions and enthronements, he faced great tests of principle and could not be swayed from his integrity. Thereupon he preserved the state and gave peace to the altars of earth and grain: supporting Emperor Zhao and setting Emperor Xuan upon the throne, Guang served as their supreme teacher and protector. Even the Duke of Zhou or <term>A-heng</term> <gloss>the Chancellor 伊尹 Yi Yin</gloss>—how could they have surpassed him?
<gloss>Shigu says: "'<term>A-heng</term>' was the official title of Yi Yin. '<term>A</term>' means to lean upon; '<term>heng</term>' means balanced and fair. This signifies that he was the one upon whom all under Heaven leaned, and from whom the multitudes below received balance."</gloss>
Yet Guang lacked formal learning and had no mastery of statecraft, remaining blind to universal moral principles. When his wife harbored depraved and wicked schemes
<gloss>Jin Zhuo says: "He did not expose or condemn her wrongdoing."</gloss>,
he installed his daughter as empress, sinking deep into overflowing desires and thereby multiplying the disasters of ruin and collapse
<gloss>Shigu says: "'<term>Zhan</term>' <note>湛</note> is read as '<term>chen</term>' <note>沈, meaning submerged or drowned</note>."</gloss>.
After his death, in barely three years, his clan and lineage were utterly exterminated
<gloss>Shigu says: "'<term>Cai</term>' <note>財</note> is the same as '<term>cai</term>' <note>纔, meaning barely or merely</note>."</gloss>.
How lamentable indeed! In ancient times, Huo Shu was enfeoffed in Jin
<gloss>Shigu</gloss>

<summary>Ban Gu appraises the career of Huo Guang, praising his steadfast loyalty in guiding young emperors and saving the dynasty, while lamenting his lack of moral learning and failure to control his family's ambitions, which brought about their annihilation.</summary>

They formulated the statute on officials failing to report known crimes, allowing supervisors to oversee and control one another. That official punishment was carried to its absolute extreme began with this.

Yu was by nature incorruptible and austere.

<note>Shigu states: "Ju" </note><note>original: 裾</note> also means arrogant and aloof. It is read identically to "ju" <note>original: 倨</note>.

Ever since he became an official, his residence never accommodated visiting guests. When the high ministers and nobility paid visits to invite him to their residences,

<note>Shigu states: "Zao" </note><note>original: 造</note> has the phonetic reading given by the fanqie spelling qian-dao.

Yu in the end never returned their calls or expressed gratitude. His goal lay entirely in severing requests from acquaintances, friends, and guests.

<note>Shigu states: He used this principle to report back to the high ministers. Liu Chang states: "Returning calls and expressing gratitude" properly belongs to the upper sentence, meaning that when high ministers paid visits to invite Yu, Yu in the end never went to them.</note>

He stood alone and pursued a single course, nothing more. Whenever he witnessed a breach of the law, he seized upon it immediately, yet he also never investigated thoroughly to unearth the secret misdeeds of subordinate officials.

<note>Shigu states: Concerning those crimes that were not directly witnessed or known, he conducted no search or pursuit.</note>

He was once dismissed midway, but later was appointed Commandant of Justice. Earlier, the Marquis of Tiao <note>Zhou Yafu</note> had considered Yu's severity deeply ingrained. By the time Yu became Privy Counselor and rose to the Nine Ministers, his methods were harsh and pressing. Toward his later years, administrative affairs grew increasingly numerous, and officials strove for severe rigor. Yu's administration, by contrast, grew more lenient, and he gained renown for fairness. Wang Wenshu and others who arose later governed with even greater harshness than Yu. Because of his old age, Yu was transferred to become Chancellor of Yan.

Shang's four sons all reached the rank of Grand Administrator. His eldest son, Li, served as Intendant of the Capital. All valued prestige and severity, and gained renown for administrative ability and eloquence.

The Appraisal states: From Zhi Du downward, all gained renown for harsh cruelty. Yet Zhi Du was unbendingly straightforward, pointing out right and wrong and contending over fundamental principles of state. Zhang Tang, through his intelligence, flattered and accommodated the sovereign, rising and falling in harmony with his mood.
<note>Su Lin says: The character for "accommodate" </note><note>original: "邑"</note> has the pronunciation of the character in "distressed acceptance" <note>original: "悒"</note>. Yan Shigu says: According to Master Su's explanation, the character 邑 is pronounced *wu-he* <note>Wu-he fan: archaic fanqie phonetic spelling</note>. However, current editions sometimes write the character for "countenance" or "expression" <note>original: "色"</note>. This means flattering and observing the sovereign's facial expressions to rise or descend accordingly. Both interpretations are viable. Song Qi says: Li Qi notes that *a* <note>original: "阿"</note> is pronounced *wu*. Xiao Gai examines the Hanshu and notes that texts reading "flattered and seduced the sovereign" <note>original: "阿媚人主"</note> represent clerical copying errors.
At timely moments he argued appropriateness, and the state relied on his expediency. Zhao Yu based himself upon the laws and preserved uprightness.
<note>Yan Shigu says: The character for "based upon" </note><note>original: "据"</note> is pronounced and read as "to rely upon" <note>original: "據"</note>.
Du Zhou practiced sycophancy, regarding speaking little as grave solemnity. After Zhang Tang's death, the legal net grew tight and state affairs piled up in thickets.
<note>Yan Shigu says: "Thickets" </note><note>original: "叢"</note> means numerous.
Officials drifted into sluggishness, waste, and decay.
<note>Yan Shigu says: "Drifted" </note><note>original: "濡"</note> means gradually sinking in. "Decay" <note>original: "耗"</note> means disorder; it is pronounced *mo-bao* <note>archaic phonetic gloss</note>.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Yu Qing abandoned his state and gave up his rank to relieve his impoverished friend Wei Qi in his distress.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: Wei Qi was a friend of Yu Qing. When Wei Qi was about to be killed by Fan Ju, Yu Qing went to rescue him.</note>

Lord Xinling, Wuji, stole the military tally, faked the ruler's command, executed the general, and usurped command of the army in order to rush to the rescue of Lord Pingyuan in his crisis.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: The troops of Qin were besieging Zhao. The chancellor of Zhao, Lord Pingyuan, sent an urgent appeal to Wuji. Wuji used Lady Ru to steal the military tally, forged King Anxi of Wei's decree to replace Jin Bi as commanding general, and ordered Zhu Hai to strike and kill Jin Bi with an iron hammer. He then led the troops to rescue Zhao. The Qin army retreated, and Zhao was preserved intact.</note>

All of them thereby gained prestige among the feudal lords and made their names renowned across the realm. Those who clasped their wrists and engaged in wandering debate took the Four Lords as their foremost champions.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: <term>E</term> <gloss>to clasp / grip</gloss> means to grasp and hold. <term>Ji</term> <gloss>wrist</gloss> was an ancient character for the wrist of the hand. The Four Lords refers to Lord Xinling of Wei and the others mentioned above. The character <term>e</term> has the pronunciation of the character meaning hardship or distress.</note>

Thereupon, discussions that turned one's back on the public interest in devotion to factional coteries flourished, while the duty of performing one's official post and revering superiors fell into ruin. When it came to the rise of the Han dynasty, the net of legal prohibitions was wide and loose, and this conduct was not yet corrected or reformed.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: <term>Kuang</term> <gloss>to rectify / correct</gloss> means to make right.</note>

For this reason, Chen Xi, chancellor of the state of Dai, travelled with a retinue of a thousand carriages; Liu Pi of Wu and the King of Huainan each recruited guests and retainers numbering in the thousands. Among imperial relatives and senior ministers, the Marquis of Weiqi and the Marquis of Wu'an...

<summary>This page recounts how prominent Warring States figures like Yu Qing and Lord Xinling sacrificed civic order to aid friends, establishing a culture of factional loyalty that persisted unchecked into the early Han dynasty.</summary>

Xian possessed wealth in the tens of millions. When he was about to depart, he left behind bedding, mats, and utensils worth several millions.

<note>Song Qi remarks: Below the character "left" </note><note>original: "留"</note>, the character "his" <note>original: "其"</note> should be present.

He wished to give them to Zhang, but Zhang would not accept them. When guests asked him the reason, Zhang sighed and said: "As a commoner, I was treated with favor by Lord Shi.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: This means he was treated with kindness and pity by Shi Xian.</note>

Now that Lord Shi's family is ruined, I have no means to keep him safe.

<note>Yan Shigu comments: This means he lacked the power to rescue him.</note>

Yet if I were to accept his wealth and property, when this has brought catastrophe upon the Shi clan, could the Wan clan perversely regard it as good fortune?" The dignitaries admired and praised him for this. During the Heping era <note>28–25 BCE</note>, Wang Zun became Governor of the Capital. He arrested and struck down knights-errant, killing Zhang along with Zhang Hui the arrow-maker,

<note>Fu Qian comments: The arrow-maker's surname was Zhang and his given name was Hui.</note>

Zhao Jundu of the wine market, and Jia Ziguang.

<note>Fu Qian comments: A man of the wine market.</note>

All of them were prominent local magnates of Chang'an who avenged personal grudges and harbored assassins.

<note>Editorial note: 次定四等十三与</note>

The Emperor traveled from Ganquan to spend the night at Chiyang Palace. When the Emperor ascended Changping, an imperial edict instructed the Chanyu not to make a formal prostration. <note>original: "師古曰不令拜也" Yan Shigu notes: He was not ordered to prostrate.</note>

His ministers, including the Left and Right Danghu officials, were all permitted to stand in ranks to view the proceedings. Tens of thousands of monarchs, chiefs, kings, and marquises of the various barbarian tribes all gathered to welcome him beneath Wei Bridge, arrayed in ranks lining both sides of the roadway. When the Emperor ascended Wei Bridge, all cried out "Long live the Emperor!" 

The Chanyu retired to his official residence, where he remained for over a month before being sent back to his state. The Chanyu personally petitioned, wishing to remain and reside below the Guanglu Pass, <note>original: "師古曰即徐自為所築者也" Yan Shigu notes: That is, the fortification constructed by Xu Ziwei.</note> and in times of emergency to seek protection at the Han Shouxiang fortress. <note>original: "師古曰保守也於此自守" Yan Shigu notes: 'Bao' means to protect and hold; here he would defend himself.</note>

### Volume 94, Part 2

<note>Yan Shigu says: The character <term>hui</term> <gloss>beak/jaw</gloss> is pronounced like <term>xu</term> combined with <term>hui</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

By the beginning of the Benshi reign <note>73–70 BCE</note>, the Xiongnu harbored treacherous and recalcitrant ambitions.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Jie</term> <gloss>obstinate/stubborn</gloss> means hard and rebellious. It signifies that they arose in disobedience.</note>

They wished to plunder the Wusun and violate the Han princess. Thereupon, five generals were dispatched leading an expeditionary army of 150,000 cavalry to hunt down the enemy across the south, while the Marquis of Changluo led 50,000 cavalry from the Wusun to strike awe throughout their western border. Both forces reached their agreed rendezvous points and returned.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>pledge/rendezvous</gloss> means good faith; it refers to the appointed place.</note>

At that time, they captured little.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Xian</term> <gloss>rare</gloss> means few; it is pronounced like <term>xian</term> combined with <term>jian</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

They merely displayed their martial prowess and manifested the might of Han forces like thunder and wind. Although they marched out and returned empty-handed, two generals were nevertheless executed for their failures. Therefore, the northern barbarians did not submit, and the Central Plains could not yet rest easy on high pillows.

When it came to the Yuankang and Shenjue eras <note>65–58 BCE</note>, great spiritual virtue and majestic grace spread widely, while internal turmoil erupted within the Xiongnu. Five Chanyu competed for the throne. Rizhu and Huhanye brought their state to submit in desperation, prostrating themselves and declaring themselves subjects.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Fu</term> <gloss>prostrate</gloss> is pronounced like <term>pu</term> combined with <term>bei</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

Yet the Han court still maintained the strategy of loose rein <note>jimi</note>, not assuming arbitrary and total control over them.

<note>Yan Shigu says: The character <term>zhuan</term> is identical with <term>zhuan</term> <gloss>monopolize/dominate</gloss>. <term>Zhuanzhi</term> <gloss>exclusive control</gloss> refers to reducing them completely to subjects and bondservants.</note>

<summary>Following minor frontier campaigns against the Xiongnu during the Benshi reign, internal civil war fractured the Xiongnu under five rival Chanyu, prompting Huhanye to submit to Han authority under the loose-rein policy.</summary>
<keywords>Hanshu, Xiongnu, Wusun, Huhanye Chanyu, Benshi, Yuankang, Shenjue, Yan Shigu, Jimi policy</keywords>

Zhu said: "Our state has only recently suffered invasion. The envoy should depart; Hu is even now preparing day and night to enter the capital and have audience with the Son of Heaven."

After Zhu departed, his ministers remonstrated with Hu, saying: "The Han raised an army to execute Ying, but in truth they also acted to intimidate Southern Yue. Moreover, the late king stated that in serving the Son of Heaven, one should strive not to fail in protocol, but the crucial point is that one must not be seduced by flattering words into entering the capital for an audience."
<gloss>Shigu says: "Chu" means to entice or induce. It means one must not be enticed and persuaded by sweet words to enter the Han court. The character is pronounced like the fanqie of xian and yu.</gloss>
"If you enter the capital for an audience, you will never be able to return; this would be the circumstance that brings ruin to our state."

Thereupon Hu claimed illness and ultimately did not go to the capital for an audience. More than ten years later, Hu fell genuinely and gravely ill. Crown Prince Yingqi requested permission to return home. When Hu died, he was given the posthumous title King Wen.

Yingqi succeeded to the throne. He immediately concealed the imperial seals of his predecessors, the Martial Emperor <note>Zhao Tuo</note> and the Civil Emperor <note>Zhao Hu</note>.
<gloss>Li Qi says: He discarded their usurped imperial titles.</gloss>

During his time in Chang'an, Yingqi had taken a woman of the Jiu clan from Handan as his wife.
<gloss>Shigu says: Jiu is pronounced like the fanqie of ju and qiu.</gloss>
She bore a son named Xing. When Yingqi ascended the throne, he submitted a memorial requesting that the woman of the Jiu clan be established as queen and that Xing be made his heir. The Han repeatedly sent envoys

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Imperial Counselor Wei Xiang <note>Song Qi notes: The Zhejiang edition lacks the character *ji* <gloss>and</gloss>.</note> appointed Wangzhi as an aide, and recommended him for honesty and integrity, leading to his appointment as Assistant to the Grand Master of Ceremonies in Charge of Rituals <term>Daxing Zhili Cheng</term>. 

At that time, General-in-Chief Huo Guang had passed away. His son Yu again became Grand Minister of War <term>Da Sima</term>, while his elder brother's son Shan took charge of the Secretariat <term>Shangshu</term> <note>Yan Shigu notes: Huo Shan was the grandson of Huo Qubing. Referring to him now as an elder brother's son is merely a scribal error in transmission.</note>. All their relatives served in the imperial night watch and as inner palace attendants. 

In the summer of the third year of Dijie <note>67 BCE</note>, hailstones fell in the capital. Taking advantage of this, Wangzhi submitted a memorial expressing his wish to be granted a leisure audience in private, so that he might explain in person the meaning of this celestial calamity. <note>Yan Shigu notes: *Jian* <gloss>interval</gloss> is read as *xian* <gloss>leisure</gloss>.</note>

Emperor Xuan, who had personally heard of Wangzhi's reputation while he was living among the common people, remarked: "Is this not Scholar Xiao from Donghai?" The Emperor referred the matter to Privy Counselor Song Ji to inquire into the circumstances. <note>Yan Shigu notes: *Ji* is pronounced with the fanqie phonetic *ju-yi*.</note> 

He told Wangzhi to conceal nothing. Wangzhi responded, arguing: "In the third year of Duke Zhao in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, heavy hail fell. At that time the Ji lineage had usurped power and eventually expelled Duke Zhao. If the ruler of Lu had observed and understood this celestial sign earlier, he could have averted such disaster. <note>Yan Shigu notes: *Xiang* is read as *xiang* <gloss>formerly</gloss>. *Wang* is read as *wu* <gloss>without / avert</gloss>.</note> Now Your Majesty has..."

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>to wail and weep in the palace halls. Those in the palace whose duty it is to mourn and wail shall do so each morning and evening, raising their voices fifteen times in wailing; when the ritual is completed,
they shall cease. Except at the designated hours of morning and evening mourning, it is forbidden to wail without authorization. Once the coffin has descended into the grave,
<note>Yan Shigu stated: "This means lowering the coffin into the tomb."</note>
<note>The phonetic reading and meaning are identical to those in the Annals of Emperor Gaozu.</note>
the mourners shall wear greater coarse hemp for fifteen days, lesser coarse hemp for fourteen days, and fine hemp for seven days, after which they shall discard their mourning garments.
<note>Fu Qian stated: "These all should properly be called <term>dagong</term> <gloss>greater mourning of coarse cloth</gloss> and <term>xiaogong</term> <gloss>lesser mourning of coarse cloth</gloss>. <term>Xian</term> <gloss>fine hemp</gloss> refers to garments of fine cloth." Ying Shao stated: "<term>Hong</term> <gloss>red/coarse cloth</gloss> refers to using red cloth for the collars and borders during the intermediate sacrifice of auspiciousness and the great sacrifice of auspiciousness. <term>Xian</term> <gloss>fine hemp</gloss> means unlined garments. In total, thirty-six days elapse before shedding mourning garments; this represents substituting days for months." Jin Zhuo stated: "It is standard practice in the Book of Han to use <term>hong</term> <gloss>red</gloss> in place of <term>gong</term> <gloss>coarse mourning cloth</gloss>." Yan Shigu stated: "<term>Hong</term> <gloss>red</gloss> and <term>gong</term> <gloss>coarse mourning cloth</gloss> are identical; the two explanations of Fu and Jin are correct. This mourning regulation was created by Emperor Wen following his own personal judgment; it was not derived from the Rites of Zhou. Why should it be regarded as substituting days for months? The three-year mourning period in fact spans twenty-seven months; where is there any text prescribing thirty-six months? Furthermore, unlined garments do not involve a period of seven months. Master Ying erred first in this regard, and subsequent scholars blindly followed this fallacious theory without examining it." Liu Ban stated: "The mourning attire instituted by Emperor Wen was strictly reckoned from the time after the burial took place. Prior to the burial, mourners wore untrimmed sackcloth <term>zhancui</term>. For the various emperors of Han, the time from demise to burial frequently exceeded one hundred days; so long as the burial had not taken place, mourning garments were not shed. In the biography of Zhai Fangjin, when his stepmother died, he returned to attend to official business thirty-six days after her burial had been completed; this serves as proof. Commentators who subsequently claimed this was substituting days for months were likewise misguided."</note>

<summary>Emperor Wen's testamentary edict establishes strict parameters for palace wailing and defines mourning attire periods lasting thirty-six days after burial, prompting detailed commentary on whether this abbreviated mourning substituted days for months.</summary>

When Emperor Xiaowen ruled over all under Heaven, he opened the passes and bridges, treating distant regions no differently than those near.

<gloss>Zhang Yan states: "In the twelfth year of Emperor Xiaowen, the border passes were abolished and travel passes were no longer used, so that both near and far were treated as one."</gloss>

He abolished laws against defamation and removed mutilating corporal punishments. He bestowed gifts upon the elderly, and cared for orphans and the childless, thereby fulfilling the lives of all living beings.

<gloss>Yan Shigu states: "<term>Sui</term> <gloss>to fulfill</gloss> means to accomplish and to bring to fruition."</gloss>

He curtailed his desires and refused tributary offerings.

<gloss>Yan Shigu states: "<term>Qi</term> is read as <term>shi</term> <gloss>desire / indulgence</gloss>."</gloss>

He did not condemn the wives and children of criminals.

<gloss>Su Lin states: "Punishment did not extend to wives and children." Yan Shigu states: "<term>Tang</term> is pronounced the same as <term>nu</term> <gloss>wife and children</gloss>."</gloss>

He did not execute the innocent, nor did he treat the empire's revenues as personal gain. He abolished castration and sent home the palace maidens, showing deep reluctance to sever a person's lineage. I am lacking in wisdom and incapable of comprehending all his virtues.

<gloss>Yan Shigu states: "<term>Min</term> <gloss>quick-witted</gloss> means intelligence and swift understanding. <term>Shengshi</term> <gloss>comprehend fully</gloss> means to know completely."</gloss>

These were deeds that earlier rulers could not achieve, yet Emperor Xiaowen carried them out in person.

<gloss>Yan Shigu states: "Earlier rulers refers to sovereign kings of antiquity."</gloss>

His virtue was as profound as Heaven and Earth, and his benevolence spread across the four seas. None failed to receive his blessings. His brightness resembled that of the sun and moon, yet the music of his ancestral temple does not match his greatness. I am deeply apprehensive."

<summary>Emperor Jing praises the virtuous governance and compassionate legal reforms of Emperor Xiaowen, expressing concern that the ancestral temple music fails to honor his achievements adequately.</summary>

Earth represents the earthly deity, whose yin nature is tranquil and still. During the season when transformation should unfold, one ought to revere it and refrain from disturbing it. I observe that since the first month, cloudy darkness has continued day after day. The Yi Neizhuan <gloss>Inner Commentary on the Book of Changes</gloss> states: "Protracted overcast skies without rain signify disordered qi; this corresponds to the portent of Meng <gloss>Obscurity</gloss>." "Meng" indicates that sovereign and minister, superior and subordinate, encroach upon and obscure one another in disorder.

<note>Prince Zhanghuai's commentary: The Yi Jilan Tu <gloss>Chart for Examining the Book of Changes</gloss> states: "The portent of a solar eclipse is when yin overtops yang; this corresponds to the portent of Meng. Yin encroaches upon yang." Zheng Xuan's commentary notes: "Meng is obscuring vapor. The portent is not singular. Treacherous ministers plot to cover and obscure their ruler. First, mist arises from dusk at night, or from midnight, or at dawn. If the sovereign does not awaken to it, and by midday it does not dissipate, it turns into Meng. If the sovereign still does not awaken, mist descends below." The pronunciation of "bi" <gloss>portent/comparison</gloss> is indicated here. Liu Ban observes: The commentary notes that "yin overtops yang"; examining this, the character "de" <gloss>obtain/overtop</gloss> should properly be written as "fu" <gloss>cover</gloss>, and following the character "yang", the character "ye" should appropriately appear.</note>

It also states: "When virtuous worthies are left unemployed, its anomaly is persistent overcast skies." Worthy individuals are the foundation of transformation, while clouds are the instrument of rain. To obtain worthy men and leave them unemployed is like persistent overcast skies without rain. According to ritual propriety, when the Son of Heaven takes a wife, he marries nine women at once, with principal wives and accompanying brides fully provided for. Now the palace ladies and attendants are numbered by the thousands. Some spend their lives in secluded corners, their natural human relations blocked. This accumulation of suppressed resentment ascends and moves August Heaven. For this reason, Heaven dispatched Mars to enter Xuanyuan, to regulate human relationships and suspend celestial signs revealing anomalies, so as to awaken the sovereign above.

In ancient times, when King Wu of Zhou stepped down from his carriage, he released the women of the Qing Palace and marked with honors the village gate of Shang Rong,

<note>The *Great Commentary to the Classic of Documents* states: "When King Wu entered Yin, he honored the village gate of Shang Rong and returned the women of the Qing Palace."</note>

thereby ordering human relationships and honoring worthy virtue. Therefore Heaven bestowed upon him a sagely son, King Cheng. Today, Your Majesty amasses palace women in great numbers, thereby defying Heaven's will. Consequently, imperial offspring mostly die young, and there is no bodily successor upon whom to rely. The *Classic of Poetry* says: "Revere the wrath of Heaven; dare not indulge in sport and pleasure."

<note>These lines are from the "Ban" hymn in the "Greater Odes" of the *Classic of Poetry*. The commentary states: "Sport and pleasure means idle indulgence."</note>

In the present day, of all blessings, none is greater than broadening the succession. To broaden

<summary>Xiang Kai argues that Mars lingering in Xuanyuan warns Emperor Huan against filling his harem with thousands of neglected women while neglecting the imperial succession.
