### Biography of Guo Ji

Guo Ji, whose style name was Xihou, was a native of Maoling in Fufeng commandery. His great-great-grandfather was Guo Jie.
<gloss>The *Book of the Former Han* states: Guo Jie, whose style name was Wengbo, was a native of Zhi in Henei commandery. He relocated during Emperor Wu's reign and was widely known as an errant knight.</gloss>
His father, Guo Fan, served as Grand Administrator of Shu Commandery. In his youth, Guo Ji already possessed ambitious purpose and upright conduct.

# Biography of Wang Tang

Wang Tang, courtesy name Jingbo, was a native of Qi in Guanghan commandery. He was initially recommended as an Outstanding Talent <term>maocai</term> by the Minister of the Household <term>guanglu</term> <gloss>Guanglu Xun</gloss>. <note>interlinear commentary: The Minister of the Household recommended him as an Outstanding Talent.</note>

He was transferred to become Magistrate of Gucheng, where his administrative governance achieved distinguished renown. <note>interlinear commentary: Gucheng county belonged to Dong commandery. Its former city was situated east of present-day Dong'e county in Qi prefecture.</note>

During the Yongchu era <note>107–113 CE</note>, the Western Qiang invaded and raided Ba commandery, causing severe distress to the people. An imperial edict was issued dispatching General of the Household <term>zhonglangjiang</term> Yin Jiu to lead a punitive campaign against them, but for successive years he could not overcome them. The Three Ducal Ministries <term>sanfu</term> <gloss>the offices of the Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works</gloss> recommended Tang as capable of managing difficult crises. He was appointed Grand Administrator of Ba Commandery. Tang galloped with his troops to confront the brigands, beheading and capturing more than one thousand of them. The regions of Ba and Yong were restored to peace and tranquility, and the officials and common folk erected a shrine in his honor during his lifetime. <note>interlinear commentary: Yong refers to Shangyong county. Its former city is situated west of present-day Qingshui county in Fang prefecture.</note>

Inspector <term>cishi</term> Zhang Qiao submitted a memorial commending his administrative abilities, and Tang was promoted to Colonel-Director of Retainers of the Right <term>youfufeng</term>. When Emperor An made an imperial tour to the west, his wet nurse Wang Sheng and the Regular Palace Attendant <term>zhongchangshi</term> Jiang Jing

When Niu Fu had met his defeat, his multitude had no one upon whom they could rely, and they wished to scatter and return home. Li Jue and his associates became fearful. Thereupon, they sent envoys in advance to Chang'an to beg and sue for imperial amnesty. Wang Yun considered that two amnesties could not be granted within a single year, and therefore did not grant it. 

Jue and the others grew increasingly fraught with apprehension and dread, not knowing what to do. Jia Xu, a native of Wuwei, was serving in Jue's army at that time and persuaded them:

<note>original: "魏志曰：卓之入洛陽，詡以太尉掾為平津尉，遷討虜校尉。牛輔屯陝，詡在輔軍。輔既死，故詡在傕軍。"</note><note>Records of Wei states: When Dong Zhuo entered Luoyang, Jia Xu served as an assistant to the Grand Commandant and was appointed Commandant of Pingjin, later being promoted to Colonel Who Subdues Bandits. While Niu Fu was stationed at Shan, Xu served in Fu's army. After Fu died, Xu consequently remained in Li Jue's army.</note>

Xu said: "I hear that people in Chang'an are discussing an intention to exterminate all natives of Liang Province. If you gentlemen abandon your army and travel alone, even a mere <term>tingzhang</term> <gloss>village constable</gloss> will be able to bind you. It is better to lead one another westward to attack Chang'an, avenging <term>Dong gong</term> <gloss>Lord Dong</gloss>. If the affair succeeds, we shall uphold the state to bring righteousness to all under heaven. If it turns out unpromising, it will not yet be too late to flee."

Li Jue and the others agreed with him. Speaking to one another, they said: "The capital refuses to pardon us; we must resolve this by risking our lives. If..."

<summary>Following Niu Fu's death, Li Jue and his commanders panic when their plea for amnesty is denied by Wang Yun, but Jia Xu persuades them to unite their forces and march west to assault Chang'an.</summary>

Secretaries in the Masters of Writing merely recorded schedules and meetings, while the Nine Ministers and Three Excellencies merely filled out the roster of offices and nothing more.

<note>Historical commentary: The Previous Book of Han records that Jia Yi said: "High officials were treated with severity merely over failure to report paperwork or schedules during meetings, which was regarded as a grave transgression."</note>

Former Grand Commandant Yang Biao had successively overseen two departments of state, holding the highest rank of the supreme governance.

<note>Historical commentary: The Continuation of the Book of Han states: 'Biao replaced Dong Zhuo as Minister of Works, and again replaced Huang Wan as Minister of Education. When Yuan Shu arrogated titles in rebellion, Cao Cao alleged that Biao was related to Shu by marriage, falsely accusing him of plotting to depose and establish an emperor. Cao Cao memorialized that he be arrested and cast into prison, charging him with high treason.'</note>

Merely out of personal spite, Cao Cao framed him on baseless charges. Whipping and torture were inflicted together, and all five cruel punishments were brought to bear upon him at once.

<note>Historical commentary: The Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian states: 'They arrested Biao, cast him into prison, and interrogated him. Subsequently, by imperial decree, he was dismissed from office.'</note>

Giving rein to his passions and unleashing his villainy, Cao Cao completely disregarded the statutory code. Furthermore, Court Gentleman Zhao Yan offered loyal admonitions and straightforward speech, submitting proposals worthy of adoption. For this reason, the sacred court listened with receptive favor, changed countenance, and bestowed honors upon him. Cao Cao, seeking to blind and usurp the discernment of the times and sever the avenue of speech, arbitrarily arrested and immediately executed him without waiting to report to the throne. 

Furthermore, King Xiao of Liang was the uterine younger brother of the previous emperor. His sepulcher was lofty and distinguished, and the pines, cypresses, mulberries, and catalpas around it ought to have been treated with reverence and solemnity. Yet Cao Cao led generals, officers, and soldiers in person to excavate the tomb, breaking open the coffin, exposing the corpse, and plundering gold

<summary>Yuan Shao's proclamation indicts Cao Cao for reducing state ministers to mere ciphers, torturing former Grand Commandant Yang Biao on fabricated charges, executing the loyal remonstrator Zhao Yan, and personally despoiling the imperial tomb of King Xiao of Liang.</summary>

The Zhi River rose dramatically. <note>Interlinear commentary: "The Classic of Waterways states that the Zhi River originates at Mount Yao, west of Luyang County in Nanyang, flows southeast past the north side of Kunyang city, and enters the Ru River to the east. In the first year of the Xingping era <note>194 CE</note>, Cao Cao launched an eastern campaign against Tao Qian, ordering his general Chen Gong, a native of Wuyang, to garrison Dong Commandery.

<gloss>The *Dianlüe* states: Chen Gong, courtesy name Gongtai, was a native of Dong Commandery. He was upright, resolute, bold, and vigorous. In his youth, he formed ties with renowned men throughout the realm. When the empire fell into chaos, he initially followed Cao Cao <note>referred to here by his posthumous title Taizu</note>, but later grew suspicious and uneasy, whereupon he turned to follow Lü Bu. Chen Gong devised strategies for Lü Bu, yet Lü Bu consistently failed to heed them.</gloss>

Chen Gong consequently persuaded Zhang Miao, saying: "Today the empire is fractured and collapsing, and heroes arise on every side. You command an army of one hundred thousand, occupying territory open to assault from all four directions.

<gloss>Chenliu is flat terrain subject to enemy attack from all four sides; therefore it is called territory open to assault from all four directions.</gloss>

With hand on your sword and a watchful glance, you have more than enough stature to be a leader of men, yet instead you find yourself subject to another. Is this not deeply humiliating? Now the provincial army has marched east on campaign, leaving the local territory completely undefended. Lü Bu is a valiant warrior, peerless and unstoppable in battle. If you welcome him and join forces to seize Yan Province, observe the shifts in the balance of power across the realm, and wait for changing circumstances, you can bestride the age as a dominant power."

Zhang Miao agreed with his counsel. He then joined with his younger brother Zhang Chao, Chen Gong, and others to welcome Lü Bu as the Governor of Yan Province and occupy Puyang. The surrounding commanderies and counties all rallied in support. When Cao Cao heard the news, he led his army back.

<summary>Chen Gong convinces Zhang Miao to rebel against Cao Cao while his forces are campaigning in the east, seizing Yan Province and welcoming Lü Bu as its new governor at Puyang.</summary>

# Biography of Wang Huan

Wang Huan, whose courtesy name was Zhizi, was a native of Qi County in Guanghan Commandery. <gloss>The ancient city of Qi County was located southwest of present-day Qi County in Zizhou.</gloss>

His father, Shun, served as Grand Administrator of Anding. In his youth, Huan was fond of chivalric knight-errantry and valued martial vigor. He frequently associated with reckless, frivolous youths. <gloss><term>Piao</term> means to plunder and seize.</gloss> Later in life, he reformed his conduct, devoting himself to Confucian scholarship. He studied the *Classic of Documents* <note>original: "Shangshu"</note> and read the statutes and ordinances, grasping their essential principles.

He served as Officer of Merit <note>senior administrative official responsible for personnel assessment and appointments in the commandery</note> under Grand Administrator Chen Chong. In discharging his official duties, he was decisive and resolute, showing no favor or leniency toward powerful and influential families. Because of this, Chong's renown and reputation spread widely, and he was summoned to the capital to serve as Grand Minister of Agriculture <note>one of the Nine Ministers of the central government, responsible for state revenues and treasury</note>.

Emperor He asked him: "What methods did you use to govern your commandery so effectively?"

Chong bowed his head to the ground and humbly replied: "Your servant entrusted matters to Officer of Merit Wang Huan to select the worthy and promote the capable, and to Chief Clerk Tan Xian to make good on omissions and rectify errors. Your servant merely proclaimed and promulgated Your Majesty's imperial edicts."

The Emperor was greatly pleased. From this, Huan's reputation became renowned. The provincial authorities recommended him as an Eminent Talent <note>a prestigious civil recommendation category, originally called Flourishing Talent</note>, and he was appointed Prefect of Wen County. The county harbored many deceitful and cunning villains who had long caused distress and suffering to the people. Huan used calculated strategies

<summary>Wang Huan reforms his youthful chivalric ways to master the Confucian classics and law, serving with fearless impartiality under Chen Chong, whose praise before Emperor He leads to Huan's appointment as Prefect of Wen County.</summary>

Item One: The Monthly Ordinances of the Hall of Distinction <note>commentary: The Son of Heaven resides in the Hall of Distinction and promulgates administrative policies in accordance with each month; hence it is called the 'Monthly Ordinances of the Hall of Distinction.' The 'Four Commencements' refer to the Beginning of Spring, Beginning of Summer, Beginning of Autumn, and Beginning of Winter. On each of these days, the Son of Heaven personally welcomes the seasonal atmospheric influences in their corresponding directional quarter, and simultaneously sacrifices to the thearch of that quarter. At the end of the final month of summer, he sacrifices to the Central Thearch.</note> provide that the Son of Heaven, at the Four Commencements and at the nodal period of late summer, welcomes the Five Thearchs in the suburban altars.

These rites serve to summon and conduct the spiritual energies, pray for blessings and an abundant harvest, perform sacrifices in the Pure Ancestral Temple, show filial reverence toward ancestors who have passed away, nourish the elderly in the Biyong Academy, and manifest ritual education to the people. All of these constitute the grand undertakings of sovereign rulers, reverently upheld by ancestral predecessors.

Yet the official functionaries, repeatedly citing distant mournings from tributary states, births within the palace apartments, and minor contaminations among clerks and soldiers, constantly invent taboos and pretexts for omission. <note>commentary: 'Minor contaminations' refers to illness and death.</note>

I observe in private that fasting and purification for the sacrifices at the Southern Suburb have never once been abandoned. Yet when it comes to other sacrificial rites, discordant arguments are raised at every turn. Could it be that the Southern Suburb is base while other sacrifices are noble? In his youth, Qiong was appointed as a cadet in the household of the Crown Prince <note>original: "太子舍人"</note> on account of his father's official privilege. He declined on grounds of illness and did not take up the post. When he encountered mourning for his father, he completed the full period of mourning rites. All five ducal offices simultaneously summoned him to their staff, yet year after year he did not answer.

During the Yongjian reign period <note>126–132 CE</note>, many dukes and ministers recommended Qiong. Thereupon, along with He Chun of Kuaiji and Yang Hou of Guanghan, he was summoned by official carriage. When Qiong arrived at Lunshi, he pleaded illness and refused to advance further.

<note>Lunshi was formerly the state of Lun in the Xia dynasty, the fief of Shaokang. The Bamboo Annals </note><note>original: "竹書紀年"</note> states: "Chu and Qin attacked Zheng at Lunshi." It is now situated at the old city wall of Songyang County in modern Luozhou.

The authorities indicted him for irreverence. An imperial edict was sent down ordering the county magistrate to console and dispatch him with ritual courtesy. He had no choice but to comply. Prior to this, many of the retired scholars who had been summoned failed to live up to public expectation. Li Gu, who had long admired Qiong, sent a letter ahead to greet him, stating:

"I hear you have already crossed the Yi and Luo rivers and are close by at the Wansui Pavilion <note>Pavilion of Ten Thousand Years</note>. Does this mean your entry into service is gradually unfolding, and that you will comply with the royal command?

<note>The Wansui Pavilion is located northwest of the old Songyang County seat in modern Luozhou. In the first year of the Yuanfeng reign </note><note>110 BCE</note>, Emperor Wu visited Goushi and ascended Mount Taishi. Later, he was summoned by official carriage to serve as Senior Clerk to General-in-Chief He Jin. He Jin feared he would not come, so he immediately recommended him to be an Imperial Attendant. When He Jin was defeated, the imperial mandates were cut off. After Emperor Xian ascended the throne, Dong Zhuo assisted in government affairs and summoned Xun Shuang once again. Xun Shuang wished to flee, but the officials in charge kept close watch over him, so he could not leave. Consequently, he accepted appointment as Chancellor of Pingyuan. When he reached Wanling, he was pursued and appointed Minister of the Imperial Household. After three days in office, he was promoted to Minister of Works. From his initial summons to ascending to the Three Excellencies, it took only ninety-five days. He then followed the court in moving the capital to Chang'an. 

Xun Shuang saw that Dong Zhuo was growing increasingly cruel and tyrannical, and would certainly endanger the state. Therefore, all those he recruited and recommended were men of talent and strategy, intending to conspire together against Dong Zhuo. He also plotted secretly with Minister over the Masses Wang Yun, Dong Zhuo's Chief Clerk He Yong, and others. Just at that time, he fell ill and died, at the age of sixty-three.

<summary>Xun Shuang cites ancient ritual canons regarding mourning, is rapidly promoted under He Jin and Dong Zhuo to Minister of Works within ninety-five days, and secretly plots with Wang Yun against Dong Zhuo before falling ill and dying at sixty-three.</summary>

<gloss>Yiyang is the name of a county, situated north of the Yi River. Its ancient fortified city lies east of modern Yiyang County in Tan Prefecture.</gloss>

They killed the county magistrate, and their multitude grew steadily larger. The court again dispatched Imperial Internuncio Ma Mu to supervise Liu Du, the Inspector of Jing Province, in attacking them. The imperial army was defeated, and Mu and Du fled. Emperor Huan issued an edict commanding the high ministers to recommend someone qualified to replace Liu Du. Minister Zhu Mu recommended Du Shang. Shang was elevated from Commander of the Right Construction Corps to become Inspector of Jing Province. Shang personally led his troops, sharing hardship and rest with them. He extensively recruited various southern tribesmen, clearly established bounties and rewards, and advanced to attack, heavily defeating the rebels. Those who surrendered numbered in the tens of thousands. The veteran rebel chieftains of Guiyang, Bu Yang and Pan Hong, feared Shang's fierce prowess and retreated into the mountain valleys. Shang pursued them relentlessly for several hundred li, entering Nanhai and destroying three of their encampments, capturing vast quantities of rare treasures. However, the faction of Yang and Hong remained formidable. Shang wished to attack them, but his soldiers had grown arrogant and wealthy, and none had any will to fight.

For this reason, the local villagers called him "Jiang the Greatly Filial" <gloss>Ju means great. Hua Qiao's book states: "Yang Yin, Magistrate of Linzi, esteemed him highly. He arranged a special place of honor to distinguish the Greatly Filial one among the assembled crowds, and personally offered money to assist in providing for his mother."</gloss>. 

The commandery grand administrator once prepared ceremonial gifts to summon Ge, but Ge declined on account of his mother's advanced age. When his mother passed away, his grief was so extreme that his vital spirit was nearly extinguished. He lay mourning inside a hut by her grave, and even when the mourning period concluded, he could not bear to remove his mourning robes. The commandery governor dispatched assistant officials to remove his mourning garments and invited him to become an official. 

In the early years of the Yongping era <note>58–75 CE</note>, he was nominated as Filial and Incorruptible and appointed as a Gentleman, and then assigned as Grand Servant to the Kingdom of Chu. After a little over a month, he impeached himself and resigned. Liu Ying, King of Chu, sent subordinate officials riding in haste to pursue him, but Ge refused to return. The King further dispatched the Grand Tutor of the Kingdom to present gifts, yet Ge declined and would not accept them. Later, though summoned repeatedly by the Three Excellencies, he promptly resigned each time. 

At the beginning of the Jianchu era <note>76–84 CE</note>, Grand Commandant Mou Rong recommended him as Worthy, Good, Square, and Upright. He was twice promoted, becoming Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works. Emperor Suzong <gloss>Emperor Zhang of Han</gloss> held him in immense reverence and esteem, promoting him to Commander of the Five Officers of the Rapid Tiger Cadets. At every court assembly, the Emperor would always order the imperial tiger-guards to assist and support him.

<summary>Jiang Ge earned the title Jiang the Greatly Filial by pulling his mother in a cart to spare her distress, mourned her death with life-threatening devotion, and later received high court honors under Emperor Zhang despite repeatedly resigning public posts.</summary>

<gloss>Brave imperial palace guards <note>original: "huben"</note> were ministers who maintained the night watch and garrisoned the palace. Attendants of robes <note>original: "zhuiyi"</note> were officials in charge of imperial attire; *zhui* <note>original: "贅"</note> means to stitch or attach <note>original: "綴"</note>, pronounced with the initial and final of *zhi* and *rui*. The *Classic of Documents* states: "Attendants of imperial robes and brave imperial palace guards." Gatekeepers and eunuch chamberlains <note>original: "hunyin"</note> as well as private apartment eunuchs <note>original: "hunsi"</note> were both eunuch officials. The *Rites of Zhou* includes gatekeepers and chamberlain eunuchs. "With halberds arrayed on the palace steps" means clutching halberds while standing upon the palace steps. "A hundred ranks" indicates great numbers. *You* means place or that which; *si* means to take charge of. For rhyme, it is pronounced like *si* <note>meaning to watch over or wait upon</note>.</gloss>

Round guard lodges in a thousand ranks, patrol lanes interlaced like patterned silk.

<gloss>Guard lodges refer to the lodging quarters of the imperial night guard stationed around the palace perimeter. "A thousand ranks" signifies great abundance. The "Statutes for the Palace Guard" in the *Records of the Grand Historian* state: "Round guard lodges were established with troops under exceedingly strict discipline." Patrol lanes were paths for making surveillance rounds. "Interlaced like patterned silk" means crisscrossing. The *History of the Former Han* states: "The Commander of the Capital Guards held charge over patrols and inspections in the capital city."</gloss>

Imperial carriage thoroughfares wind and turn; extended roadways and soaring pavilions rise aloft.

<gloss>The *Phonetic Meanings of the History of the Former Han* says: "Carriage thoroughfares refer to raised corridors and elevated walkways." *Tu* <note>original: "涂"</note> also means road <note>original: "塗"</note>; these ancient characters were interchangeable.</gloss>

Reaching out from the Weiyang Palace to connect with the Gui Palace, extending northward past the Mingguang Palace and linking across to the Changle Palace; crossing over stepped pathways and rising above the western city wall; joined together with the Jianzhang Palace as an outer annex; erecting the Phoenix Watchtowers of the Jade Gate, where high upon the ridge beams roost golden sparrows.

<gloss>The Weiyang Palace lay in the west, while the Changle Palace lay in the east. The Gui Palace and Mingguang Palace lay in the north. This describes elevated walkways interconnecting them. *Deng* refers to the flight of steps, pronounced with the initial and final of *ding* and *deng*. *Yong* means the city wall. *Hun* means unified together. The Jianzhang Palace was situated west of the walled city; *shu* means connected. The *History of the Former Han* states: "To the east of the Jianzhang Palace stood the Phoenix Watchtower Gate, over twenty *zhang* high; to its south stood the Jade Gate and its annexes." The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "*Guling* refers to the highest vantage point atop a palace hall." *Gu* is pronounced like *gu*; *ling* is pronounced like... <note>original: "欠三句半之旨", the commentary text breaks off here with three and a half sentences missing</note></gloss>

Has anyone ever not been enabled <note>to perform the sacrifices</note>, relying merely on bamboo and silk writings without magnifying laws and standards, or leaving behind texts without performing the Feng and Shan? How could it be only with regard to me that this alone is omitted?

*Yi* means *wei* <note>an initial particle, "now" or "contemplating"</note>. *Suigu* is like *yuangu* <gloss>profound antiquity</gloss>. The *Songs of Chu* <note>original: "Chuci"</note> states: "At the beginning of profound antiquity..." *Li* means to arrive. This means: from profound antiquity down to the present. "Those who have undertaken" refers to those who performed the Feng and Shan sacrifices. The *Records of the Grand Historian* <note>original: "Shiji"</note> states that Guan Zhong said: "From ancient times, seventy-two rulers performed the Feng and Shan." Adding Emperor Wu and Emperor Guangwu, they make seventy-four rulers. *Bi* means to cause or enable. Possessing the realm under Heaven without being enabled to perform the Feng and Shan, while relying merely on writings upon bamboo and silk: there has never been one who magnified laws and standards, or left behind literary compositions, who omitted the Feng and Shan sacrifices.

*Tai* means me or myself. "How could it be with regard to me that this alone is omitted?"

At this time, the Sage Sovereign had already concentrated his refined spirit and wandered in contemplation, gathering all literary arts. Repeatedly he consulted the gathered scholars and took counsel with venerable elders, deliberating with them upon the deep source of the Way and Virtue, and examining the vast thicket of benevolence and righteousness, in hope that the primal auspicious tokens would arrive.

"Sage Sovereign" refers to Emperor Zhang. *Yu* means to inform; *zi* means to deliberate and counsel. Because the Way, Virtue, benevolence, and righteousness are what people constantly practice, they are compared here to drink and food. "Deep source" and "vast thicket" are metaphors for profound depth. *Yuan* means Heaven. *Fu* means auspicious omen. The *Classic of Poetry* states: "The meats and dried fruits are set out in order." *He* <note>覈</note> also means dried fruits and seeds <note>核</note>, referring to the category of fruits.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Qing moved out to reside in his own mansion. The Emperor bestowed upon him three hundred male and female slaves, carriages and horses, money and silk fabrics, bedcurtains and canopies, precious treasures, and luxury curios, completely filling his residence. He also granted money and silk fabrics, graded according to rank, to everyone from the junior tutor <gloss>zhongfu</gloss> down to the personal attendants.

<note>The Sound and Meaning of the Book of Han states that "junior tutor" <term>zhongfu</term> is the name of an official post.</note>

Qing suffered frequently from illnesses and was at times in poor health. Morning and evening, the Emperor inquired after his condition and sent meals and medicines, caring for his needs with the utmost thoroughness. Qing was exceedingly cautious, respectful, and filial. Because he had previously been deposed as crown prince, he was especially fearful of overstepping and strictly adhered to the laws. Whenever he attended court or paid visits to the imperial mausoleums and ancestral temples, he would regularly rise at midnight, dress meticulously in his formal robes and cap, and await the break of dawn.

<note>"Midnight" <term>yefen</term> means half of the night.</note>

He strictly instructed his subordinate officials that they must not race their carriages and horses against those of the other imperial princes. He constantly felt secret grief and resentment over the deficiencies in the funeral rites accorded to his mother, the Imperial Noble Consort. Whenever the four seasonal sacrifices, the summer sacrifice, and the winter ancestral sacrifice came, he always conducted sacrifice in his private chambers. Only after the Dou clan was purged did he send his wet nurse to perform distant sacrifices to her north of the city wall. When Grand Empress Dowager Dou passed away, Qing petitioned to visit his mother's tomb to express his mourning. The Emperor granted permission and decreed that the imperial grand providore should provide sacrificial utensils for the four seasons. Qing wept with tears streaming down his face,

In the twelfth year of the Jian'an reign <note>207 CE</note>, he was murdered by the Yellow Turban rebels. His son Kai succeeded to the title. He reigned for thirteen years. When the Wei dynasty received the abdication, he was made the Marquis of Chongde.

### Biography of Shu, the Mourned King of Chengyang

Shu, the Mourned King of Chengyang, was enfeoffed in the second year of the Yongyuan reign <note>90 CE</note>, when a portion of Jiyin was separated to form his kingdom. He reigned for five years and died. He was buried in the capital city. Having no sons, his princedom was eliminated, and its territory was reunited with Jiyin.

### Biography of Wansui, the Youthful King of Guangzong

Wansui, the Youthful King of Guangzong, was enfeoffed in the fifth year of the Yongyuan reign <note>93 CE</note>, when a portion of Julu was separated to form his kingdom. In that same year he died, and was buried in the capital city. Having no sons, his princedom was eliminated, and its territory was reunited with Julu.

The historian's appraisal states: The Book of Rites records five forms of remonstrance, among which indirect admonition <note>original: "fengjian"</note> ranks highest.

<note>Commentary notes: The five forms of remonstrance are indirect admonition, compliant admonition, watchful admonition, direct pointing admonition, and peril admonition. Indirect admonition means perceiving the sprout of misfortune and disaster, and conveying warning through subtle analogy. Compliant admonition means offering words that are humble and yielding, not defying the ruler's inner sentiment. Watchful admonition means observing the sovereign's facial expression before presenting admonition. Direct pointing admonition means pointing straightforwardly at the matter itself when remonstrating. Peril admonition means speaking out on that which brings peril to the state.</note>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and held sway over the imperial harem.

At first, Honorable Lady Song gave birth to Imperial Crown Prince Qing, and Honorable Lady Liang gave birth to Emperor He. Since the Empress had no son of her own, she was jealous and resentful of both of them, and repeatedly sowed discord between them and the Emperor. Gradually, estrangement and suspicion arose. She then falsely accused Honorable Lady Song of practicing sorcery and seductive black magic. Honorable Lady Song subsequently committed suicide, and Qing was deposed as the Prince of Qinghe. The account is found in Qing's biography.

Honorable Lady Liang was the daughter of Liang Song. She lost her mother at an early age and was raised by her paternal aunt, the Senior Princess of Wuyin.

<gloss>The Senior Princess was the daughter of Emperor Guangwu; Liang Song married her.</gloss>

At the age of sixteen, in the second year of Jianchu <note>77 CE</note>, she and her elder sister were both selected to enter the <term>yeting</term> <gloss>women's quarters of the imperial palace</gloss> as Honorable Ladies. In the fourth year <note>79 CE</note>, she gave birth to Emperor He. The Empress raised him as her own child. Wishing to keep the honor and prestige of being the imperial maternal family exclusively for herself, she resented and feared the Liang clan. In the eighth year <note>83 CE</note>, she fabricated an anonymous slanderous letter to frame Liang Song.

<gloss>An anonymous slanderous letter is equivalent to what is now called an anonymous letter.</gloss>

Liang Song was implicated and executed, while the Honorable Lady and her sister died of grief and sorrow. From this time on, the concubines and palace women held their breath in terror.

<summary>Empress Dou schemes against Honorable Ladies Song and Liang to eliminate rivals and claim Emperor He as her own child, causing the death of both consorts and the destruction of the Liang clan. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>economy, so contemporaries rarely valued him. He often dreamed of a mulberry tree growing out of a well, and consulted Zhao Zhi, an interpreter of dreams. 

Zhi said: "A mulberry tree is not something found inside a well; it will surely be transplanted elsewhere. However, the character for mulberry <term>sang</term> <gloss>桒</gloss> is composed of 'forty' with 'eight' below. I fear your lifespan will not exceed this." Zhi laughed and said: "To reach that is quite enough for me!"

Earlier, after serving in the commandery, he became an Attendant Officer for Military Supervision <term>dujun congshi</term> <gloss>督軍從事</gloss>. At that time, Zhuge Liang enforced the laws with severity and strict precision. Liang privately heard that Zhi engaged in amusements, was self-indulgent, and neglected his duties. Liang once went unexpectedly to inspect the prisoners and prison records. Everyone was terrified on Zhi's behalf. Zhi secretly caught wind of this; at night he lit the lamps, examined the prisoners, and read all their petitions and case summaries. 

When Zhuge Liang arrived early in the morning, Zhi had already memorized and recited every detail, answering questions and explaining matters without the slightest hesitation or delay. Liang was greatly astonished by him.

He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Chengdu. At that time, the position of Magistrate of Pixian was vacant, so Zhi was appointed to oversee both counties simultaneously. The households and populations of the two counties were dense and numerous; being close to the capital seat, they were rife with wicked and corrupt deeds. Zhi would regularly appear to be sound asleep, yet the moment he awoke, he would immediately detect fraudulent and treacherous acts. Everyone feared his uncovering and exposure of wrongdoing, and some even believed he possessed supernatural arts, so that none dared deceive him. When people were made to cast counting rods to perform calculations, Zhi simply listened to them recite the figures and calculated them in his head, not erring by so much as a sheng or a he <note>units of dry measure, equivalent to a fraction of a liter</note>. His sharp acumen was of this degree.

The Yi people of Wenshan grew restless, so Zhi was appointed Administrator of Wenshan. Both the Chinese commoners and the Yi submitted to and trusted him. Later, he was transferred to Guanghan. Afterward, the Yi rebelled, and their messengers declared: "Only if we obtain our former Governor He can we be pacified." 

At that time, it was difficult to reassign Zhi back, so they promoted one of Zhi's kinsmen to govern Wenshan, and the region once again achieved peace. Zhi was later transferred to become Administrator of Qianwei. At the age of forty-eight he passed away, just as Zhao Zhi had predicted.

Later, Wang Li of Guanghan, whose style name was Boyuan, also became prominent through his talent and administrative ability. He served as an Attendant Officer for Military Supervision, applying the laws with fairness and balance. He was gradually promoted to succeed Zhi as Administrator of Qianwei, and his administration had an excellent record. Although his intelligence did not equal that of Zhi, his literary talent surpassed him.

<summary>He Zhi demonstrates remarkable administrative ability, memory, and popularity among the border peoples, fulfilling a prophecy of his lifespan, and is succeeded in Qianwei by the talented Wang Li.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>cruelly devoured and swallowed the eight regions of the realm. Thereupon horizontal and vertical alliances <note>original: "從橫", referring to the <term>zong</term> <gloss>vertical</gloss> and <term>heng</term> <gloss>horizontal</gloss> diplomatic alliances during the Warring States period</note> arose like swirling clouds, and deceit and imposture multiplied like scattered stars. Perverse and strange notions swarmed like bees, and craft and guile sprouted forth. Some adorned truth to pass off falsehood, some clung to wickedness to solicit glory, some took to deceitful paths to extort favors from their superiors, and some peddled their skills in self-glorification. They turned their backs on the upright and venerated the wicked, abandoning straightness to associate with flatterers. Loyalty lacked fixed duties, and righteousness possessed no constant rule.

Therefore, when Shang Yang's laws reached their limit, vicious wickedness broke out <note>original: "鞅法窮而慝作", referring to Lord Shang (Shang Yang), the Legalist reformer whose harsh laws ended with his execution and rebellion</note>; when Li Si's schemes failed, treachery was accomplished <note>original: "斯義敗而姦成", referring to Li Si, Chancellor of Qin, whose machinations led to disaster under the Second Emperor</note>. The gate of Lü Buwei was grand, yet his clan was extinguished <note>original: "呂門大而宗滅", referring to Lü Buwei, Chancellor of Qin and wealthy patron who was forced to commit suicide</note>; Han Fei's persuasive arguments were established, yet his body suffered execution <note>original: "韓辨立而身刑", referring to Han Fei, the preeminent Legalist philosopher who was imprisoned and compelled to drink poison</note>.

For what reason did this happen? Profit seduced their hearts, and favored honors dazzled their eyes. Their dragon-embroidered robes shone resplendently, their carriages and garments were dazzling and bright. Indulging in reckless fortunes and base gain, they acted with fickle whims and reckless capsizing. Licentious, perverse, dissolute, and deluded, their willful insolence reached its utmost extreme. Yet before the bells on their carriage were even tuned, their bodies already lay beside the carriage shafts; before their feet could tread the courtyard and inner hall, the ridgepole snapped and the rafters collapsed. Heaven withdrew its vital essence, Earth shrank its moistening bounty, men lamented their physical ruin, and spirits sheared their foreheads. <summary>Xi Zheng describes the chaotic moral decline of the late Zhou and Qin periods, citing historical figures like Shang Yang, Li Si, Lü Buwei, and Han Fei who pursued selfish ambition and fleeting glory only to meet ruin.</summary>

Yang Fu submitted a memorial, stating: "In ancient times, King Wen received the auspicious sign of the red crow, yet even as the sun inclined in the afternoon he had no leisure to eat. When King Wu had a white fish leap into his boat, ruler and ministers turned pale with apprehension before taking action. Even upon receiving auspicious omens, they still maintained anxiety and reverence. How much more should one tremble with caution when celestial disasters and anomalies occur!

"Presently Wu and Shu are not yet pacified, while Heaven repeatedly sends down changes in signs. Your Majesty ought to dedicate your utmost attention to responding to them, sitting attentively on the edge of your mat and contemplating how to display virtue to those afar, and pacify those near through frugality. <summary>Emperor Ming commends Yang Fu's frank counsel and promotes him to Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues. Hu Zhi <note>original: "胡質"</note>, styled Wende <note>original: "文德"</note>, was a native of Shouchun in the state of Chu <note>original: "楚國壽春", in modern Anhui</note>. In his youth, he, Jiang Ji, and Zhu Ji were all well-known between the Changjiang and Huai rivers, and he served in the regional and commandery administrations. 

When Jiang Ji served as Aide-de-Camp <note>original: "别駕", Biejia</note>, he was sent on an embassy to meet the Grand Ancestor <note>original: "太祖", Cao Cao</note>. 

The Grand Ancestor asked him: "Hu Tongda is a senior man of broad understanding. Does he happen to have sons or grandsons?" 

Jiang Ji replied: "He has a son named Zhi. In grand scope and broad design, he does not measure up to his father; but when it comes to meticulous skill and managing affairs, he surpasses him."

<note>According to the Genealogical Record of the Hu Clan </note><note>original: "胡氏譜"</note>, Tongda's given name was Min, and he was summoned to office on account of his uprightness and rectitude.

The Grand Ancestor immediately summoned Hu Zhi and appointed him Magistrate of Dunqiu <note>original: "頓邱令"</note>. 

A commoner of the county named Guo Zheng committed adultery with his female cousin and murdered her husband, Cheng Ta. A commandery clerk, Feng Liang, was imprisoned as a material witness. Guo Zheng and the cousin were both resilient under torture and concealed their guilt, while Feng Liang, unable to endure the agony of interrogation, made a false confession and was on the verge of taking the blame for their crime. 

When Hu Zhi arrived in office, he observed their countenances and examined the case in greater detail. Upon proper investigation and cross-examination, they all confessed their crimes. 

He was subsequently brought into the central administration as an Assistant Secretary of the East Bureau to the Chancellor <note>original: "丞相東曹議令史"</note>. Later, the regional administration requested his transfer to serve as Attendant Officer <note>original: "治中", Zhizhong</note>. 

At that time, General Zhang Liao had an estrangement with his Army Supervisor, Wu Zhou.

<summary>This passage introduces Hu Zhi, recording Jiang Ji's recommendation of him to Cao Cao, his astute resolution of a murder and false confession case in Dunqiu, and his subsequent administrative appointments.</summary>
<keywords>Hu Zhi, Cao Cao, Jiang Ji, Dunqiu, legal case, Sanguozhi, Zhang Liao, East Bureau, Han dynasty</keywords>

In the end, Sun Quan was indeed unable to march out.

At that time, Cao Shuang held monopolistic control of state power, and moral standards declined. Wang Ji composed the <term>Shiyao Lun</term> <gloss>Treatise on Current Essentials</gloss> to sharply address contemporary affairs. He was recalled to court due to illness and was subsequently appointed Intendant of Henan. Before he could assume office, Cao Shuang was executed. Because Wang Ji had served as a subordinate under Cao Shuang, he was dismissed from office according to standard precedent.

Later that year, he was appointed Imperial Secretary and then transferred out to serve as Inspector of Jingzhou, with the additional title General Who Manifests Fierceness. He accompanied Wang Chang, the General Who Conquers the South, on an expedition against Wu. Wang Ji led a separate force to launch a surprise attack on Bu Xie at Yiling. Bu Xie shut the gates and mounted a defense. Wang Ji feigned an assault while secretly detaching troops to capture the granaries at Xiongfu. He seized more than three hundred thousand <term>hu</term> <gloss>bushels</gloss> of grain, captured Tan Zheng, the General Who Pacifies the North, and received the surrender of several thousand people. Thereupon, he relocated these surrendered people and established Yiling County. He was granted the noble rank of Marquis of Guannei.

Wang Ji also memorialized the throne, proposing to build a fortress at Shangchang and move the seat of Jiangxia Commandery there to exert pressure on Xiakou. Consequently, the enemy dared not cross the Yangtze River lightly. He clarified institutional regulations, organized military affairs and agriculture, and cultivated schools.

<summary>Wang Ji criticizes Cao Shuang's corrupt regime through his writings, experiences a brief dismissal following Shuang's fall, and is soon restored to high provincial and military office. Leading forces against Eastern Wu alongside Wang Chang, he outmaneuvers Bu Xie at Yiling, captures vital supplies and enemy officers, strengthens the border defenses along the Yangtze, and promotes civil administration.</summary>
<keywords>Wang Ji, Cao Shuang, Shiyao Lun, Wang Chang, Jingzhou, Bu Xie, Yiling, Xiongfu, Tan Zheng, Jiangxia, Xiakou, Three Kingdoms, Wei dynasty</keywords>

Furthermore, in its rear garden, a scenic tower and ancestral temple were erected for his mother's maternal lineage, and the neighborhood was named Weiyang Lane to express perpetual longing for his mother's clan. In the first month of the third year of the <term>Jiaping</term> <gloss>reign era of Cao Fang, 251 CE</gloss> era, Chang died. He was posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry and given the posthumous name Marquis Gong. His son Zhen Shao succeeded him.

In the sixth year of the <term>Taihe</term> <gloss>reign era of Cao Rui, 232 CE</gloss> era, Emperor Ming's beloved daughter Cao Shu passed away. She was posthumously titled and honored as Princess Yi of Pingyuan, and a dedicated temple was established for her. The Emperor took the deceased grandnephew of Empress Zhen, Zhen Huang, and buried him jointly with her, posthumously ennobling Huang as a Ranked Marquis. He appointed Lady Guo's maternal younger cousin, Guo Hui, to be Huang's successor, taking on the surname Zhen, and enfeoffed Hui as Marquis of Pingyuan to inherit the princess's noble title.

Sun Sheng remarked: According to the rites, women possess no precedent for receiving noble enfeoffments; how much less should an infant in early childhood be enfeoffed with a great city? Hui was from a different clan, recruited as a successor across distinct kinship lines: possessing neither merit nor blood relation, he nevertheless inherited a mother's title. Transgressing moral affection and violating classic ritual was never more extreme than in this case. Although Chen Qun voiced strong protests and Yang Fu cited historical precedents to draw comparisons, neither could thoroughly expound the rites of the ancient sage kings or clarify the fundamental principles of feudal ennoblement and lineage succession. In their sincere and loyal words, was there not still something lacking? The Book of Songs states: "Majestic Grand Master Yin, the people all gaze up to you." How could the responsibilities of the prime ministers and imperial advisors be thus neglected? The *Biographies of Notable Figures of Jin* states: Hui

<summary>Emperor Ming commemorates Empress Wenzhao's clan by founding Weiyang Lane, and later creates an unprecedented succession upon the death of Princess Yi of Pingyuan, drawing severe historical criticism from Sun Sheng.</summary>

Zhang said to his attendants: "A true man should serve like Wei Qing and Huo Qubing <note>famous Western Han dynasty generals who fought against the Xiongnu</note>, commanding one hundred thousand cavalry across the desert to drive back the Rong and Di barbarians, winning military renown and establishing great fame. How could one merely become an academician <gloss>boshi, an imperial court scholar</gloss>?"

Taizu <note>Cao Cao</note> once asked his sons what they enjoyed, instructing each to declare his ambition. Zhang said: "I wish to become a general."

Taizu said: "What must one do to become a general?"

Zhang replied: "Wear sturdy armor, grip sharp weapons, face danger without looking back, lead the soldiers from the front, ensure rewards are unfailingly bestowed, and ensure punishments are unfailingly carried out."

Taizu laughed heartily.

In the twenty-first year of Jian'an <note>216 CE</note>, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yanling. In the twenty-third year <note>218 CE</note>, the Wuhuan tribes of Dai Commandery rebelled. The court appointed Zhang as General of the Household of the North <gloss>Bei Zhonglang Jiang</gloss>, acting as General of Agile Cavalry <gloss>Xiaoqi Jiangjun</gloss>.

Just before he set out, Taizu admonished Zhang, saying: "At home, we are father and son; when undertaking public duty, we are lord and minister. Every action must conform to the royal laws: take heed of this!"

Zhang marched north and entered the territory of Zhuo Commandery. Rebel barbarians numbering several thousand cavalry suddenly arrived. At that time, Zhang's troops and horses had not yet assembled, and he had only one thousand infantrymen.

<summary>Cao Zhang expresses his martial ambitions to emulate the great Han generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing rather than pursue scholarly learning. Appointed by Cao Cao to quell the Wuhuan rebellion in Dai Commandery, he faces a surprise attack by thousands of enemy cavalry with only a fraction of his forces assembled.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>You are an outstanding talent of the realm; entering court, you attend upon the imperial gate, and stepping forth, you ascend to the nine executive ranks <note>original: "九列" (jiulie), the Nine Ministers</note>. Your commanding presence imposes order upon Qing and Xu provinces, and your inspiring influence spreads to the borders of Wu. In former days we mistakenly shared the same rank; our deep friendship surpassed that between the states of Lu and Wei. Separated now for more than ten years, my longing for you from afar grows ever tighter in my heart. I hope you will recognize this sincerity, and that our pledge will endure unchanged through winter cold and summer heat."

Shi Chong replied: "In the past, I often joined your retinue, and together we roamed among the azure clouds. We cultivated the moral Way to instruct the scions of state; the Confucian transformation shone brightly and harmonized all. Having the same voice, there was no discordant echo; thus our mutual affection grew deep and grand. How could it merely be an earnest beginning? Our genuine fellowship must be preserved to a noble end. Confucius did not look down upon the Nine Barbarian Tribes <note>original: "九夷" (Jiuyi)</note>, and Laozi journeyed to the Western Rong <note>ancient non-Chinese peoples to the west</note>. Wandering freely along the shores of the vast blue sea, one can surely preserve one's royal person. Worldly affairs are not what should occupy us, and the Duke of Zhou is no longer worth dreaming about. Profound tranquility makes the spirit reign supreme; therefore I abide in the utmost emptiness."

The <term>Jin Shu</term> <gloss>Book of Jin</gloss> by Wang Yin records that Li Chong, Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, submitted a memorial stating: "The imperial clan of the Wei dynasty remains submerged and stagnant, yet they are always remembered by Your Majesty's sacred grace. The Administrator of Dongwan, Cao Jia, possesses talent, learning, and righteousness that do not quite equal those of Zhi and Xi; however, his integrity and purity of character, as well as his moral nature and conduct, surpass theirs. Furthermore, he has already governed two commanderies. Your subject considers that, in giving precedence to the descendants of the preceding dynasty, Jia may be appointed as Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant Gentleman <note>original: "員外散騎侍郎" (yuanwai sanqi shilang)</note>."

Qin, Prince Shang of Gang <note>Prince Shang of Gang indicates one who died young, receiving the posthumous name Shang</note>, died prematurely. In the fifth year of Taihe, he was posthumously granted an enfeoffment and posthumous title. He left no heirs.

Cheng, Prince Shang of Gucheng, died prematurely. In the fifth year of Taihe, he was posthumously granted an enfeoffment and posthumous title. He left no heirs.

Zheng, Prince Dai of Mei, served as successor to his paternal cousin, Court Gentleman Shao. In the twenty-second year of Jian'an, he was enfeoffed as Prince of Mei.

<summary>This page concludes the poetic exchange between Cao Jia and Shi Chong, cites Li Chong's memorial recommending Cao Jia for office under the Jin dynasty, and records the brief biographical entries of Cao Qin, Cao Cheng, and Cao Zheng.</summary>

The *Book of Wei* <note>original: "魏書"</note> states: Initially, when the Han court relocated, the old precedents and records of the imperial secretariats <note>original: "臺閣"</note> were scattered and lost. After the capital was established at Xu, order and discipline were gradually restored. Ji corrected and settled many matters based on ancient principles. At that time, although the generals west of the Pass appeared externally to submit, inwardly they could not yet be trusted. The Colonel of the Retainers Zhong Yao requested to lead three thousand troops into the Pass, outwardly on the pretext of punishing Zhang Lu, but inwardly to coerce them into sending hostages. Taizu sent Xun Yu to consult Ji. Ji believed: "The various generals of the west are all vulgar men who rose from obscurity, with no ambition to dominate the realm, seeking only temporary ease and comfort for the present. Now the state has generously bestowed titles upon them, satisfying their desires. Unless there is some major incident, we need not worry that they will cause rebellion. We should plan for the long term. If we send troops into Guanzhong under the pretext of punishing Zhang Lu, since Lu is in deep mountains where paths and tracks are blocked, they will surely suspect it. Once alarmed, with the rugged terrain and their strong forces, the outcome will be perilous and difficult to foresee." Yu submitted Ji's counsel to Taizu. Taizu initially approved it, but because Yao was in direct charge of that responsibility, he ultimately followed Yao's advice. As soon as the troops advanced, the region west of the Pass erupted in massive rebellion. Taizu personally led an expedition and only barely pacified it, with the dead numbered in the tens of thousands. Taizu regretted not following Ji's counsel, and because of this valued Ji even more.

After the state of Wei was established, Ji was appointed Palace Attendant <note>original: "侍中"</note>, overseeing institutional rules and ceremonial systems alongside Wang Can. When Emperor Wen <note>Cao Pi</note> ascended the royal throne, Ji was transferred to Master of Writing. Shortly afterward, he returned to the Han court as an Imperial Attendant <note>original: "侍郎"</note>, where he advocated and praised the righteous principle of dynastic abdication, drafting the imperial proclamations and edicts. When Emperor Wen ascended the imperial throne, Ji again became Master of Writing.

<summary>Wei Ji restores administrative order in the capital and accurately predicts that Zhong Yao's military maneuver will trigger a massive rebellion in Guanzhong. Following the pacification of the region, Ji receives high honors, helps codify state institutions, and assists in the transition of authority to Emperor Wen of Wei.</summary>
<keywords>Wei Ji, Zhong Yao, Xun Yu, Cao Cao, Cao Pi, Emperor Wen of Wei, Wang Can, Guanzhong rebellion, Book of Wei, Sanguozhi, institutional reform, dynastic succession</keywords>

Yuan Shao, styled Benchu, was a man of Ruyang in Runan. His high-great-grandfather, Yuan An, served as Minister over the Masses <note>original: "司徒" (situ), one of the Three Excellencies, the highest civil administrative office in Han China</note> for the Han dynasty. From An downward, four generations occupied positions among the Three Excellencies <note>original: "三公" (sangong), the three highest ministerial posts in the imperial government</note>; because of this, their influence shook the entire realm.

Hua Qiao's <term>Book of Han</term> <gloss>Han shu</gloss> states:
An was styled Shaogong. He was fond of learning, dignified, and grave. During the reign of Emperor Ming, he served as Grand Administrator of Chu Commandery, where he presided over the judicial case of the King of Chu. Those whose grievances he investigated and redressed numbered more than four hundred families, and all were preserved and spared. An subsequently became a renowned minister. In the reign of Emperor Zhang, he reached the rank of Minister over the Masses. He fathered Jing, Grand Administrator of Shu Commandery. Jing's younger brother Chang served as Minister of Works <note>original: "司空" (sikong), one of the Three Excellencies</note>. Jing's son was Tang, Grand Commandant <note>original: "太尉" (taiwei), the supreme military commander among the Three Excellencies</note>. Tang had four sons: the eldest was Ping; Ping's younger brother was Cheng, Left General of the Household, both of whom died early; Cheng's younger brother was Feng, and Feng's younger brother was Kui, both of whom became Excellencies.

The <term>Book of Wei</term> <gloss>Wei shu</gloss> states:
From An downward, all were broadly benevolent and accommodated the multitude, making no distinctions among them. When guests entered their doors, whether wise or foolish, all attained what they desired; thus the entire realm turned toward them.

Shao was a concubine-born son of Feng, and an elder brother to Yuan Shu by a different mother. He was adopted out as heir to Cheng.

The <term>Records of Heroes</term> <gloss>Yingxiong ji</gloss> states:
Cheng was styled Wenkai. In his prime, he was disciplined and commanded respect. Imperial relatives and powerful magnates, from General-in-Chief Liang Ji downward, all formed friendships with him, and none failed to heed his words. Therefore, the people of the capital made a proverb about him, saying: "When a matter does not proceed smoothly, speak to Cheng and it is resolved."

Dong Zhuo summoned Shao to deliberate, wishing to depose the Emperor and enthrone the Prince of Chenliu. At this time, Shao's uncle Yuan Wei held the office of Grand Tutor <note>original: "太傅", one of the highest ministerial offices in the Han court</note>. Shao pretended to agree to his proposal, saying: "This is a momentous affair. Let me withdraw and deliberate it with the Grand Tutor."

Zhuo replied: "The stock of the Liu clan is no longer worthy of preservation!"

Shao made no reply; he brandished his sword, made a deep bow, and departed.

The <term>Xiandi Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals of Emperor Xian</gloss> states:卓 Zhuo wished to depose the Emperor and addressed Shao, saying: "The Emperor is young and dim-witted, unfit to be lord of ten thousand chariots <note>a classical expression denoting the emperor of a vast realm</note>. The Prince of Chenliu is superior; now I wish to enthrone him. A person may possess little intelligence when young, yet grow up foolish. Who can know what he will become later? For now we must proceed in this way. Do you not look to Emperor Ling as an example? Thinking upon this fills one with indignation and bitterness."

Shao said: "The House of Han has ruled the realm for some four hundred years; its favors and bounty have run deep and copious, and the millions of common folk have looked up to it in allegiance for long ages. Although the present Emperor is young and tender, no misconduct of his has been made known to the realm. If you wish to depose the legitimate son and establish the offspring of a concubine, I fear the multitude will not assent to your proposal."

Zhuo said to Shao: "Boy! Are the affairs of the realm not decided by me? When I act today, who dares not obey? Do you suppose Dong Zhuo's blade is dull?"

Shao said: "Are the stout and valiant men beneath Heaven only Lord Dong?"

He drew his belt-dagger, bowed with hands clasped across his chest, and marched out.

Your servant Songzhi observes: At that time, Shao and Zhuo had not yet formed an open breach or enmity; for this reason Zhuo consulted with him on his plans. If simply because of a disagreement in counsel Zhuo had immediately reviled him as a boy and harbored the intent to draw a weapon against him, and Shao had then answered with such extreme obstinacy and defiance, how could Zhuo have tolerated it?

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Whenever alarms were raised and urgent pursuits launched against bandit invaders, he was always at the front. He was merely literate and had little talent for administrative paperwork.

He conspired with He Jin to execute the various court eunuchs <note>original: "黃門", Huangmen, meaning Palace Attendants</note>, and was appointed Bearer of the Gilded Mace <note>original: "執金吾", Zhi Jinwu</note>.

When Jin met defeat, Dong Zhuo entered the capital. Planning to instigate rebellion, Zhuo wished to kill Yuan and incorporate his troops. Because Bu was trusted by Yuan, Zhuo enticed Bu and ordered him to slay Yuan. Bu severed Yuan's head and presented it to Zhuo. Zhuo made Bu Cavalry Commandant <note>original: "騎都尉", Qi Duwei</note>, treating him with great affection and trust, and they swore an oath to be father and son. Bu was skilled in mounted archery, and his physical strength surpassed other men; people called him the Flying General <note>original: "飛將", Feijiang</note>. In time, he was promoted to General of the Household <note>original: "中郎將", Zhonglang Jiang</note> and enfeoffed as Marquis of Duting <note>original: "都亭侯", Duting Hou</note>. Zhuo knew that he treated people discourteously and feared that someone would conspire against him; whether moving about or staying put, he always had Bu guard him. However, Zhuo's nature was unyielding, narrow-minded, and quick to wrath; he acted without considering consequences. Once, suffering a slight dissatisfaction, he drew a hand-halberd <note>original: "手戟", shouji</note> and hurled it at Bu. Bu dodged it with agile reflexes.

<note>quoting Pei Songzhi's commentary citing the Classic of Poetry</note> The Classic of Poetry states: "Without fist, without courage, they serve only as the ladder to rebellion." The commentary explains that "fist" signifies strength.

Bu apologized to Zhuo and placated him, whereupon Zhuo's anger also subsided. From then on, Bu secretly resented Zhuo. Zhuo frequently ordered Bu to guard the central private quarters, where Bu engaged in an illicit affair with Zhuo's maidservant.

He set out eastward toward his commandery, but <term>Taizu</term> <gloss>Cao Cao</gloss> had already arrived in Yan Province. Shang therefore went south to rely on Yuan Shu. When Shu usurped the imperial title, he wished to make Shang his Grand Commandant, yet did not dare say so openly, instead sending someone privately to hint at it. Shang showed no inclination to bend, and Shu did not dare force him either. In the early Jian'an era, Shang escaped to return home, but was murdered by Shu. Later, Shang's funeral procession arrived at the capital at the same time as that of Grand Tutor Ma Ridi. The Son of Heaven praised Shang's loyalty and heroic sacrifice, sighing in lamentation for him. He ordered the hundred civil and military officials to attend his funeral rites and offer sacrifices, and appointed Shang's son Wei as a Gentleman of the Palace, while Ridi was denied such honors.

The *Heroes' Chronicles* records: "Lu Bu descended eastward by land and water. When his army reached a point forty <term>li</term> <gloss>approx. 10 miles</gloss> west of Xiapi, Liu Bei's Household General, Xu Dan of Danyang, dispatched Master of Records Zhang Kuang by night to visit Bu. Kuang said: 'Zhang Yide <note>Zhang Fei</note> and the Chancellor of Xiapi, Cao Bao, quarreled with one another. Yide killed Bao, and the city is thrown into great turmoil, with none trusting one another. There are one thousand Danyang troops garrisoned inside the Western White City Gate. Hearing that the General has arrived in the east, young and old alike leap for joy as if granted new life. If the General marches your troops toward the city's west gate, the Danyang army will immediately open the gates to admit you.' 

Bu then advanced through the night and arrived beneath the city walls at dawn. At daybreak, the Danyang soldiers fully opened the gates and admitted Bu's forces. Bu sat above the gate while his infantry and cavalry set fires, heavily routing Yide's troops. He captured Liu Bei's wives and children, his military provisions, and the households of his subordinate officers and soldiers.

In the sixth month of the first year of the Jian'an era <note>196 CE</note>, at midnight, Bu's subordinate general Hao Meng of Henei rebelled. In ancient times, the downfall of Jie and Zhou was caused by wicked women <note>King Jie of Xia and King Zhou of Shang were ancient tyrants whose dynasties collapsed, traditionally blamed on their infatuation with seductive consorts Meixi and Daji</note>; the turmoil under King You and King Li arose from favored concubines <note>Rulers of the Western Zhou dynasty whose misrule and favoritism, notably toward Bao Si, led to disaster</note>. The former emperor <note>Sun Quan, founding emperor of Eastern Wu</note> observed this and took it as a personal warning. Therefore, he kept no seductive or corrupting beauties at his side, and his rear chambers held no vast accumulation of neglected women. Today the inner palace houses women by the tens of thousands, yet Your Majesty does not assign them proper ranks of consorts. Outside, unmarried men are many, while women lament within. That the wind and rain violate their proper seasonal patterns arises precisely from this imbalance. This is the fifth reason why Your Majesty does not follow the former emperor.

The former emperor toiled and worried over ten thousand state affairs, yet still feared making errors. Since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have idled in the rear palace and been bewitched by women, causing government affairs to be widely neglected and subordinate officials to harbor corruption. This is the sixth reason why Your Majesty does not follow the former emperor.

The former emperor deeply valued simplicity. His robes were not made of pure, lavish silks, his palace had no towering terraces, and his furnishings had no carved ornaments. For this reason, the state was rich, the people were well-supplied, and villainy and theft did not arise. Yet Your Majesty levies requisitions across the provinces and commanderies, exhausting the wealth and labor of the people. Soil is draped in dark and yellow silks, and the palace is adorned in vermilion and purple. This is the seventh reason why Your Majesty does not follow the former emperor.

Hu Kang, the Chief of Jiuyang, captured a surrendered insurgent named Zhou Yi. Yi was an old wrongdoer who, pressed by hardship, had emerged only temporarily, inwardly plotting rebellion. Kang bound Yi and sent him under guard to the government office. Because Kang had violated his orders, Ke forthwith executed him as a public example, reporting the circumstances in a memorial to the throne.

When the people heard that Kang had been executed merely for arresting someone, they realized the authorities only wished for them to emerge, nothing more. Taizu <note>Cao Cao</note> was unable to feel at ease because of this. When he campaigned against Sun Quan, he submitted a memorial requesting that Yu inspect and comfort the army at Qiao. He then detained Yu there, appointing him as Palace Attendant and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, bearing credentials to take part in the military affairs of the Chancellor. When Taizu's army reached Ruxu, Yu fell ill and remained at Shouchun, dying of grief and melancholy at the age of fifty. He was granted the posthumous title of Jing <gloss>Reverent</gloss>. In the following year, Taizu finally became Duke of Wei.

The <term>Wei Shi Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals of the Wei Clan</gloss> states: Taizu sent Yu a food vessel. When Yu opened it, it was completely empty. Thereupon he drank poison and died. In the second year of Xianxi <note>265 CE</note>, he was posthumously granted the office of Grand Commandant.

The Separate Biography of Yu states: From the time Yu became Prefect of the Masters of Writing, he regularly submitted written memorials regarding affairs of state. Near his death, he burned and destroyed all of them. Therefore, his extraordinary stratagems and confidential plans could not all be heard. At that time, military expeditions and systemic reforms were underway, and many old institutions were revived. Yu once said to Taizu: "In ancient times, Emperor Shun separately commanded Yu, Ji, Xie, and Gao Yao to assess all achievements; moral education and military campaigns were employed at the same time. At the beginning of Emperor Gaozu's reign, when weapons and armor were in heavy use, he still promoted people who could skillfully educate and instruct the populace. Jia Xu, courtesy name Wenhe, was a native of Guzang in Wuwei. In his youth, no one recognized his abilities, except Yan Zhong of Hanyang, who found him extraordinary and said that Xu possessed the marvelous talent of Liang and Ping <note>Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, chief strategists to Han founder Liu Bang</note>.

The <term>Jiuzhou Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals of the Nine Provinces</gloss> states:
In the first year of Zhongping <note>184 CE</note>, General of Chariots and Cavalry Huangfu Song crushed the Yellow Turbans, and his prestige shook the realm.

Yan Zhong, having been dismissed as Magistrate of Xindu, sought to persuade Song, saying: "That which is difficult to obtain yet easy to lose is opportunity. That which arrives and allows no hesitation is a turning point. Therefore, the sage always acts according to the times, and the wise necessarily take advantage of turning points to launch their actions. Now, General, you have encountered a rare fortune and stepped upon an easily resolved turning point. Yet if you walk upon fortune without grasping it, and face a turning point without acting, how will you enjoy great renown?"

Song said: "What do you mean?"

Zhong replied: "The Way of Heaven shows no favoritism; the common people align with capability. Therefore, one who achieves extraordinary merit does not accept reward from an ordinary ruler. Now, General, you were granted the battle-axe in early spring and gathered your success in late winter. Your military movements were like spirits, and your plans never required a second calculation. Within ten days, divine troops swept like lightning. Assaulting fortifications was easier than snapping dry branches, and overthrowing enemies was swifter than pouring hot water upon snow. Rolling across seven provinces, you slaughtered three hundred and sixty thousand troops, utterly leveling the army of Yellow Turbans and removing the calamity of wickedness and harm. Some seal their doors and carve stones, turning south to declare themselves king."

<summary>Xun You is posthumously honored as Marquis Jing, followed by the introduction of Jia Xu, whose early genius was recognized by Yan Zhong as comparable to Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, leading into Yan Zhong urging Huangfu Song to seize power after crushing the Yellow Turbans.</summary>

When the barbarian scout cavalry saw this, they truly believed that the great army had departed. <term>Taizu</term> <gloss>Cao Cao</gloss> ordered Chou to lead his followers and act as guides. They ascended Mount Xuwu, emerged through Lulong, passed through Pinggang, and mounted Bailangdui. When they were slightly over two hundred <term>li</term> <gloss>Chinese miles, roughly 50 miles</gloss> from Liucheng, the barbarians finally became alarmed. The <term>Chanyu</term> <gloss>supreme chieftain of the northern nomadic confederations</gloss> personally came forward to oversee the battle lines. Taizu engaged them in battle and thereupon achieved a great victory with massive beheadings and captures, pursuing the fleeing enemy north as far as Liucheng. When the army returned and entered the frontier passes, merit was assessed and enfeoffments were granted: Chou was enfeoffed as a neighborhood marquis <note>original: "亭侯"</note> with a fief of five hundred households.

The <term>Xianxian Xingzhuang</term> <gloss>Biographical Records of Past Worthies</gloss> records Taizu's memorial evaluating Chou's merit, which stated:

His literary refinement and grace are abundant and complete, while his loyalty and martial spirit are conspicuous. He is gentle in nurturing those below him and cautious in serving those above him. Measuring the times and judging the principles of things, his advances and retreats accord with righteousness. When You Province first fell into turmoil, and the northern nomads and Chinese gathered in confusion, families were scattered and displaced with nowhere to place their trust or refuge. Chou led his clansmen to take refuge in Mount Wuzhong, resisting Lulong to the north and defending the strategic passes to the south. In purity, stillness, obscurity, and seclusion, they plowed before eating. The people transformed and followed him, all joining together to provide for and support him. 

When the power and prestige of Yuan Shao and his sons extended over the northern plains, they formed ties far off with the <term>Wuhuan</term> <gloss>nomadic tribe</gloss>, acting together in concert from head to tail. Time and again they summoned Chou, but he never succumbed or bent. Later, when your subject received the imperial command and encamped his army at Yi County, Chou drove swiftly on his own initiative to arrive and lay out the strategic disposition for punishing the northern nomads. It was like Guangwu establishing the strategy against Yan <note>referring to Kuang Si advising Han Xin during the Chu-Han Contention</note>, or Master Xue assessing Huainan. He also dispatched his private retainers carrying your subject's official proclamation to lead and guide the grand army's march.

<summary>Cao Cao's northern strike catches the nomadic forces off guard via Tian Chou's mountain route, resulting in a crushing victory near Liucheng and Chou's enfeoffment. Cao Cao's official memorial commends Tian Chou's upright moral character, his peaceful refuge in Mount Wuzhong, his refusal to serve the Yuan faction, and his indispensable strategic guidance in the campaign against the northern nomads.</summary>
<keywords>Tian Chou, Cao Cao, Taizu, Mount Xuwu, Lulong, Pinggang, Bailangdui, Liucheng, Chanyu, Wuhuan, Xianxian Xingzhuang, Mount Wuzhong, Yuan Shao, military campaign, northern expedition</keywords>

# Volume 11

<meta>continues from previous page: Moreover, I specially received an imperial rescript sealed with the imperial signet...</meta>
appointing your subject as the <term>Guangluxun</term> <gloss>Minister of the Household</gloss>. Your Majesty personally embodies industrious humility, drawing comparisons to the Zhou and Qin dynasties, diminishing what is above to benefit those below. On the day your subject received this imperial command, my vital spirits scattered in disarray, and I found nowhere to hide or lay down my life. 

Your subject closely reflects upon himself: my virtue does not match that of the Four Worthies of Mount Shang <note>Yuan and Qi, who were honored with comfortable carriages by Emperor Gaozu</note>, yet I have received the honor of a comfortable carriage; my merit does not compare to that of Dou Rong <note>a general honored with imperial seal-wrapped edicts</note>, yet I have received the favor of an edict under the imperial seal. With the inferior timber of small rafters and crossbeams, I have been burdened with the duty of a pillar and ridgepole. With a life already nearing its demise, I have obtained a rank among the Nine Ministers <note>literally "Nine Thorny Trees", ancient symbol for high ministerial office</note>. I fear bringing about the misfortune of an ill omen like the phantom drumming of Zhu Bo <note>a Han official who rose too quickly beyond his merit, accompanied by portents of drum sounds</note>. 

Furthermore, age and illness encroach day by day, constantly worsening without any relief. I am incapable of being supported onto a carriage to take to the road, and thereby unable to fulfill this supreme duty. Gazing with longing toward the palace gates, I linger in heart around the imperial court. Respectfully bowing, I submit this memorial to state my feelings, begging for Your Majesty's sorrowful consideration: restrain Your generous grace and permit my release, so that my decaying bones may not be left abandoned in the open thoroughfares.

From the Huangchu era <note>220–226 CE</note> to the Qinglong era <note>233–237 CE</note>, imperial summons were issued continuously. In the eighth month of every year, gifts of oxen and wine were bestowed upon him. An imperial edict questioned Cheng Xi, the Inspector of Qingzhou: "Is Ning truly holding firmly to high moral integrity, or is he genuinely debilitated and worn down by old age and illness?"

<summary>Guan Ning declines his appointment as Minister of the Household, citing his unworthiness compared to ancient exemplars and pleading for release due to declining health, while imperial summons continue across multiple reigns.</summary>
<keywords>Guan Ning, Guangluxun, Four Worthies, Dou Rong, Zhu Bo, Cheng Xi, Qingzhou, Cao Rui, Emperor Ming of Wei, imperial summons, Sanguozhi</keywords>

釐摸畫謹毖令民畏則用剛寬和令民慕則用柔今酌由
俗之政使徒謂剛柔相濟則剛柔名猶兩存未化惟寓癉
于彰卽彰爲癉以威尋不得以恩尋亦不得何剛何柔共
渾化于不可知之域始稱不剛不柔葢使民猶存畏慕情

亦只求其協心心所運爲道道所敷爲政政所溥爲澤同

配嫁於濯銘小兒某遂閉戶剪髪以明無意雖君子
棄絕分無見期而當初之心死不自替他日父母隣
其志復欲馳白於君値君累娶張韓二氏理不可遣

者知君有愛子之意婦人匪薄不足以懽厚永心故
因君愛子以託賤質未知君意如何愁懼兼心不能
自解君附書之日笑謂妾曰他日歸洞庭愼無相避
誠不知當此之際君豈有意於今日之事乎其後季
父請於君君固不許君乃誠將不可邪抑忿然邪君
其話之毅曰似有命者僕始見君於長涇之隅枉抑
憔悴誠有不平之志然自約其心者達君之𡨚餘無

### 泉隨筆

<meta>continues from previous page: the heading "Method for finding the base and height from the hypotenuse and the base-sum difference" ended the previous page; this problem belongs to it.</meta>
Problem: the hypotenuse is forty-five, and the difference between the base and the height-hypotenuse sum is fifty-four. What are the base and the height? Answer: the base is twenty-seven, the height thirty-six. Method: I, Tong, say: square the hypotenuse to get two thousand and twenty-five; double it to get four thousand and fifty, as the dividend. Take the difference between the hypotenuse and the given difference, leaving nine, which is the base-height difference. Square it to get eighty-one, and subtract it from the dividend, leaving three thousand nine hundred sixty-nine. Extract the square root to get sixty-three, which is the base-height sum. Add the base-height difference to get seventy-two; halve it to get the height. Subtract the base-height difference from the base-height sum, leaving fifty-four; halve it to get the base.

Method for finding the base and height from the hypotenuse and the height-sum difference
<note>small-character gloss in the original:</note> The height-sum difference is the difference between the height and the sum of base and hypotenuse.

Problem: the hypotenuse is forty-five, and the difference between the height and the base-hypotenuse sum is thirty-six. What are the base and the height? Answer: the base is twenty-seven, the height thirty-six. Method: I, Tong, say: this is the same as the method for the hypotenuse and the base-sum difference. For the hypotenuse differs from fifty-four, the difference between the base and the height-hypotenuse sum, by nine; and the hypotenuse differs from thirty-six, the difference between the height and the base-hypotenuse sum, also by nine.

<summary>Base and height are found from the hypotenuse and the base-sum difference, using the doubled square of the hypotenuse to recover the base-height sum. The height-sum difference case is shown to reduce to the same method, since both yield a base-height difference of 9.</summary>
