<meta>continues from previous page: the problem of the walled town with a tree outside the north gate</meta>the south gate 14 bu, then turning and walking west 1,775 bu, one just catches sight of the tree along a diagonal line. Question: how long is the side of the town? Answer: 250 bu. Method: Zhongtong comments: the 20 bu outside the north gate is one remaining short leg; the 14 bu outside the south gate is the other remaining short leg; the westward walk is the long leg; and the side of the town is the side of the inscribed square. <note>This is the same configuration as the previous example. Solving x(x + 34) = 2 × 20 × 1,775 = 71,000 gives x = 250 bu, the side of the town. "Zhongtong comments" refers to the author, Fang Zhongtong, adding his own explanation.</note>
Method for Finding the Large Long Leg from a Small Right Triangle and the Large Short Leg
Example: The small long leg Bing–Ding is 100, the small short leg Ding–Wu is 25, and the large short leg Yi–Bing is 312.5. Question: how long is Jia–Yi, the large long leg? Answer: 1,250. Method: take the large short leg as the dividend and the small short leg as the divisor; dividing gives the large long leg. <note>The two triangles are similar, so the large long leg equals the large short leg multiplied by the small long leg and divided by the small short leg: 312.5 × 100 ÷ 25 = 1,250. The text states only the division; the multiplication by the small long leg, 100, is understood.</note>

<summary>This page finishes a walled-town problem in which a tree seen from outside the gates fixes the side of a square town at 250 bu. It then opens a new method that uses similar right triangles to find a large long leg from a small triangle and a large short leg.</summary>

Xin-Bing, the small broken gou, is 120. How long is the large gou? Answer: Jia-Yi, the large gou, is 30,000. Method, by Tong: multiply the large measuring gu of 1,350 by the large broken gou of 402 to get 542,700. Divide this by the measuring gou of 900 to get 603 as the shadow difference. Subtract the small measuring gu of 600 from it, leaving 3 as the divisor. Subtract the small measuring gu from the large measuring gu, leaving 750. Multiply this by the small broken gou of 120 to get 90,000 as the dividend. Dividing the dividend by the divisor gives 30,000, Jia-Yi, the large gou.

The principles explained here allow later scholars to clearly see that the mystery of the <term>Taiji</term> <gloss>Great Ultimate</gloss> does not belong to the categories of being or non-being, nor is it confined to any physical form or spatial dimension. If one can see through to this truth, one will realize that this elder <note>referring to Zhou Dunyi</note> truly attained the secret that has remained untransmitted since the time of the thousand sages. It is not merely a matter of building a house on top of a house or stacking a bed upon a bed <note>an idiom for redundant or unnecessary repetition</note>. To insist currently that this is not the case is because the principle is not yet understood, leading to an inability to fully grasp the meaning of his words; this is the third point.

As for the <term>Great Commentary</term> <gloss>Dazhuan, a section of the I Ching</gloss>, it already states that "that which is above form is called the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>Way</gloss>." Yet it also says, "the succession of one <term>Yin</term> and one <term>Yang</term> is called the Way." Could this truly mean that Yin and Yang are themselves above form? In fact, it is precisely to show that although one Yin and one Yang belong to the realm of physical vessels <note>concrete, formed things</note>, the reason behind the alternating sequence of Yin and Yang is the activity of the substance of the Way itself. Therefore, when speaking of the ultimate extremity of the Way's substance, we call it the <term>Taiji</term> <gloss>Great Ultimate</gloss>. When speaking of the flowing manifestation of the Great Ultimate...

<summary>Zhu Xi explains that the Great Ultimate transcends the physical realm and existence itself, clarifying that while Yin and Yang have form, the principle governing them is the formless Way.</summary>

On the Numerical Interweaving of the River Map <note>original: "River Map" or "He Tu," an ancient cosmological diagram</note>
In Response to Dong Shuzhong

This section states that the numerical values of the River Map <note>He Tu</note> are formed by the alternating sequence of odd and even numbers, and thus do not differ from the numbers of the Luo Scroll <note>Luo Shu</note>.

Dong asked: The numbers of the River Map are nothing more than the interweaving of one odd and one even number. Therefore, the position of Great Yang <note>the sun or supreme yang</note> is the number of Great Yin <note>the moon or supreme yin</note>; the position of Lesser Yin is the number of Lesser Yang; the position of Lesser Yang is the number of Lesser Yin; and the position of Great Yin is the number of Great Yang. One sees how Yin and Yang alternate and interweave, which is the process of generation and completion. As for the numbers Five of Heaven and Ten of Earth residing in the center, the Ten of Earth is simply the completion of the Five of Heaven.

<summary>Zhu Xi discusses the mathematical relationship between the River Map and the Luo Scroll, explaining how the alternating positions of Yin and Yang numbers represent the natural process of creation.</summary>
<keywords>River Map, He Tu, Luo Scroll, Luo Shu, Yin and Yang, numerology, Cosmology, Zhu Xi, Dong Shuzhong</keywords>

This section explains that the numbers are <term>canwu cuozong</term> <gloss>intermingled and complexly interwoven</gloss> such that they are universally connected. They harmonize naturally without needing any artificial arrangement.

Your previous letter also stated that one should not intermingle the numbers of the <term>Dayan</term> <gloss>Great Expansion, referring to the fifty yarrow stalks used in divination</gloss> with the numbers of the <term>Hetu</term> <gloss>Yellow River Chart</gloss> and the <term>Luoshu</term> <gloss>Inscriptions of the River Luo</gloss>. There is an explanation for this as well. While numbers each represent a specific principle, their intermingling and universal connection is something beyond human capability to create. Where they do not fit, one certainly cannot force them together; however, where they must fit, they align perfectly like two halves of a tally, no matter how they are turned or flipped. Man cannot forcibly separate them. If you can perceive this principle of natural harmony that requires no deliberate arrangement, only then will you realize that the workings of nature are so divine, subtle, and ingenious that they are almost amusing. It is truly beyond words. Returning to normalcy, the divine spirit and vital energy <term>shenqi</term> <gloss>spirit and breath</gloss> are <term>fancu</term> <gloss>numerous and hurried</gloss>, tending toward contraction and departing from expansion. Zhang Hua, in his poem Responding to He Shao, wrote: In quiet detachment, I suffer from a lack; yet in the midst of <term>fancu</term> <gloss>multiplicity and haste</gloss>, there is always a surplus. Xie Yanzhi, in his Eulogy for the Recluse Tao, wrote: He abandoned <term>fancu</term> <gloss>the complex and hurried world</gloss> to achieve simplicity and leisure. Du Fu wrote in a poem: You youngsters lightly endure the heat; for my sake, you bear with the <term>fancu</term> <gloss>bustle and pressure</gloss>. It is also written as <term>fancu</term> <note>using a different character for cu</note>. Ji Kang, in his Rhapsody on the Zither, wrote: Sometimes sparse and echoing, sometimes <term>fancu</term> <gloss>numerous and rapid</gloss>, overlapping and crowding, vertical and horizontal, interlacing and pursuing one another in a swift retreat. Fu Xiuyi, in his Rhapsody on the Capital, wrote: Coiling like dragons and snakes, winding and bending, rotating at the tip of the pole and circling at the center, following the strict rhythm of the

# Numerous and Hurried <note>Original: Fancu</note>

### Tightened Bridge <note>Original: Zhucu</note>
In an ancient poem: How sad the sound is; when the strings are tight, one knows the bridge is <term>zhucu</term> <gloss>pushed close/tightened</gloss>. Su Shi wrote in a poem: The short zither's strings are <term>zhucu</term> <gloss>pressed tight</gloss>.

### Distressed and Hurried <note>Original: Qicu</note>
Li Bai wrote: The sparrows cry out in the empty granary; for their own lives, how <term>qicu</term> <gloss>distressed and hurried</gloss> their plans are.

### The Days and Months are Hurried <note>Original: Riyue Cu</note>
In the Record of Rituals <note>Liji</note>: For Great Officers, Officers, and commoners, the encoffining occurs after three days and the burial after three months. The Commentary states: The rituals for Great Officers and Officers are lower in rank, so the funerary goods are fewer. Furthermore, their duties are <term>cuju</term> <gloss>urgent and hurried</gloss>, and righteousness allows for the curtailment of mourning; thus the <term>riyue cu</term> <gloss>days and months are hurried</gloss>. In the Book of Tang, Biography of Liu Zongyuan: Zongyuan was a close friend of Xiao Mian. In a letter to him, he said: Since coming here, I feel the <term>riyue</term> <gloss>days and months</gloss> are increasingly <term>cu</term> <gloss>hurried</gloss>, becoming more so every year. In total, life is no more than a few dozen winters and summers.

### Knees Frequently Pressed <note>Original: Xi Lü Cu</note>
Su Shi wrote in a poem: The pavilion is small, and our <term>xi lü cu</term> <gloss>knees are frequently pressed together</gloss>.

### Expanded: Distant or Hurried <note>Original: Shecu</note>
In the Book of Documents: One does not fear the poison of war whether it is far or near. The Commentary states: Far and near refers to <term>shecu</term> <gloss>distant or hurried</gloss>, speaking of whether the harm arrives late or early. In the Traditions of the Perfected Ones of Great Harmony: Some discuss the methods of the <term>shecu</term> <gloss>long or short</gloss> cycles of the movements of Heaven, Earth, the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars.

### Urgency <note>Original: Pocu</note>
In the Spring and Autumn Annals: The Duke and the Duke of Song met at Qing. The Annotation states: "Meeting" refers to a schedule made in haste. The Commentary states: Haste implies an intention of <term>pocu</term> <gloss>urgency</gloss> and lack of leisure. In the Book of Han, Biography of Liu Mai, King Gong of Liang: Mai's grandson Liu Li killed someone. The Emperor sent the Minister of Justice to interrogate him. Li, in fear, replied: I have often received imperial grace and been granted pardons. Now I know I have murdered Palace Attendant Cao. As the winter months are <term>pocu</term> <gloss>pressing and short</gloss> <note>referring to the season for executions</note>, I cling to life and fear death. Thus I feigned collapse and pretended to be ill, hoping by luck to survive for a moment. I now answer with the truth and await my punishment.

<summary>This page catalogs classical Chinese phrases related to the concept of haste, urgency, and the compression of time or space, drawing from poetry, ritual texts, and historical biographies.</summary>
<keywords>fancu, haste, time, funerary ritual, Su Shi, Li Bai, Zhang Hua, Spring and Autumn Annals, Book of Han</keywords>

<meta>The text is from the Peiwen Yunfu, a major Qing dynasty rime dictionary and encyclopedia of literary allusions. This section compiles historical and literary phrases ending in the character "du" (篤), which signifies sincerity, depth, or seriousness.</meta>

<note>original: "樂而巳得與之同憂饗天下以豐利而我得與之共害利博則丨丨樂逺則憂深"</note>
...happiness, and I only gain from sharing their worries. When the world is provided with abundant profit, I share in the harm. If the profit is vast, then the **joy is deep** <note>original: "樂篤" (ledu)</note>; if happiness is distant, then the worry is profound.

**Declining health is deep** <note>original: "衰篤" (shuaidu)</note>
Lu Yun, in a letter to Yang Yanming:
Yanxian spoke of your illness. As one moves toward **declining health being deep**, the arrival of sickness should meet the expectations of a hundred years. Although this is not necessarily a cause for doubt, the mutual compassion between relatives is a shared feeling.

**Sincerity is deep** <note>original: "欵篤" (kuandu)</note>
Lu Yun, in a funeral oration for Chen Bohua:
In the past, my shared duties with the Great Lord were **deeply sincere**. The growing love and grace were added as if toward brothers.

**Spirit is deep** <note>original: "神篤" (shendu)</note>
Lu Yun, in a poem:
The sky is gauged with light; the earth is measured without limit. When the **spirit is deep**, there is such blessing. The foundation is manifest and can flourish.

**Respect is deep** <note>original: "敬篤" (jingdu)</note>
Pan Yue, in a eulogy for Yang Zhongwu:
Once **respect was deep**, then love was also deep.

**Heaven is deep** <note>original: "天篤" (tiandu)</note>
Emperor Jianwen of Liang, in a memorial:
I humbly consider that Your Majesty’s love and harmony are profound in grace. The cherry-birch <note>a metaphor for brotherly affection</note> is **deeply heavenly**.

**Pure and deep** <note>original: "醇篤" (chundu)</note>
Zhu Xi, in a postscript for Vice Censor-in-Chief Zhao’s deeds:
The grandson of Vice Censor-in-Chief Lord Zhao showed me this volume of writings. Lord Zhao’s filial piety, prudence, and **pure depth** of character were such that even the ancients would find them difficult to match.

**Du Du** <note>proper name of a Han dynasty scholar</note>
Book of the Later Han, Biography of Ma Fang:
The Ma brothers were noble and prosperous, with assets worth hundreds of millions. Guests rushed to them from all four directions. Several hundred people of the circle of **Du Du** from the capital region were constantly dining guests at their gate.
Also, in the Biographies of the Garden of Literature:
**Du Du** was widely learned in his youth but did not cultivate minor etiquette. He lived in Meiyang and befriended the Magistrate of Meiyang. He frequently made requests of the Magistrate, which were not granted, leading to mutual resentment. The Magistrate, out of spite, arrested Du and sent him to the capital. It happened that the Grand Marshal Wu Han passed away. Emperor Guangwu ordered the scholars to write a eulogy. Du composed a eulogy while in prison, which was deemed the finest. The Emperor admired it, granted him silk, pardoned his punishment, and he eventually served as a Commandery Scholar.

**Li Du** <note>proper name of a Han dynasty figure known for righteousness</note>
Book of the Later Han, Biography of Zhang Jian:
Zhang Jian became a fugitive and wandered about. In Donglai, he stayed at the home of **Li Du**. Mao Qin, the Magistrate of Waihuang, arrived at the gate leading armed soldiers. Du led Qin inside and said to him: Zhang Jian is famous throughout the world. His flight is not due to a crime. Even if Jian could be captured, would you not fear the consequences of seizing him? Qin then stood up, patted Du, and said: Su Boyu felt ashamed to be the only gentleman; how could you, sir, monopolize all the benevolence?

<summary>This page lists literary and historical phrases ending in the character "du," signifying depth or sincerity, including biographical accounts of the scholars Du Du and Li Du from the Han dynasty.</summary>
<keywords>Peiwen Yunfu, Lu Yun, Du Du, Li Du, Han dynasty history, Chinese literary allusions, philology</keywords>

The bull could not move, and after a long time, it tried to gore him but ultimately <unclear>failed</unclear>. The villagers were amazed, and they slaughtered the cow to feed <note>Dang</note>.

In the Forest of Changes <note>Yilin</note>, it says: a lame cow <unclear>on the ridge</unclear> cannot carry grain.

In Chao Zhongzhi's poem responding to the monk Fa Yi: The autumn elk <unclear>in the pen</unclear> gains strength from the glue <note>likely referring to deer-horn glue</note>; the spring musk enters the navel, and the soot produces fragrance.

In Huang Tingjian's Eulogy for Master Juefan Planting Bamboo: Listen to the wind, listen to the rain, watch them become dragons; even if the cows and sheep <unclear>enter the pen</unclear>, they become the morning meal.

In Zhou Bangyan's Rhapsody on the Capital Bian <note>Biandu Fu</note>, the commentary says: The distinction of the river <unclear>at the pen</unclear>'s mouth.

### Sun Horns <note>Rijiao: a protrusion on the forehead considered a sign of future emperorship in physiognomy</note>

In the Book of the Later Han, Annals of Emperor Guangwu: Guangwu had a prominent nose and <term>Sun Horns</term>. Zheng Kangcheng's commentary states: Sun Horns refer to the bone in the center of the forehead rising up, shaped like the sun.

In the History of the Southern Dynasties, Annals of Emperor Wu of Liang: At birth, there was an extraordinary light; his appearance was unique, with <term>Sun Horns</term> and a dragon's face. Also, in the Annals of Emperor Gaozu of Chen: He had <term>Sun Horns</term> and a dragon's face, and his hands reached below his knees.

In the Old Book of Tang, Biography of Zheng Gai: Gai's auspicious omens matched the star spirits, and the signs opened with <term>Sun Horns</term>. He built a great furnace in a sacred era and achieved many successes in enlightened times.

In the Book of Tang, Biography of Tang Jian: Gaozu once summoned him for advice. Jian said: You, sir, have <term>Sun Horns</term> and a dragon-like court <note>forehead</note>. Your surname accords with the prophecies, and the eyes of the world have been fixed upon you for a long time.

Also, in the Biography of Li Jue: Just as he reached adulthood, he sat for the examination on the classics. Li Jiang, the Prefect of Huazhou, saw him and said: With <term>Sun Horns</term> and a pearl-like court <note>forehead</note>, you are no ordinary man. The status of a classicist is too mediocre for you.

In the Classic of Filial Piety, Divine Accordance: Fuxi had large eyes, a nose like a mountain, <term>Sun Horns</term>, and a brow like a string of pearls.

In the Records of Southern Yan: Murong De was the youngest son of Qiu. At eighteen, he was eight feet and two inches tall. On his forehead, he had <term>Sun Horns</term> and a crescent moon pattern.

In Liu Jun's Essay on Discerning Fate: A dragon's nose and <term>Sun Horns</term> are the signs of emperors. River-like eyes and tortoise-shell patterns are the appearance of dukes and marquises.

In Shen Yue's Preface to the Collected Works of Emperor Wu of Liang: A lord with <term>Sun Horns</term> emerges from among the scholars; a ruler with a sharp crown mastered ancient learning in his youth.

### Clear Note <note>Qingjiao: a high-pitched or pure musical note</note>

In the Book of the Later Han, Biography of Liu Kun: In his youth, Kun practiced etiquette and rites. During the reign of Emperor Ping, he studied the Shi version of the Book of Changes under Dai Bin of Pei. He was skilled at playing the elegant lute <note>qin</note> and knew the <term>Clear Note</term> assistant.

In the Liezi: Shi Wen of Zheng followed Shi Xiang to play the lute. Although he had Master Kuang's <unclear>Clear Note</unclear>...

Silver Ingot <note>original: "銀錠" (Yín Dìng)</note>
The *Pure Records of the Grotto Heaven* <note>original: "洞天清錄" (Dòngtiān Qīnglù)</note> states that during the reign of Emperor Taizong <note>reigned 976 to 997 CE</note>, a search was ordered for the ink calligraphy of the ancients. Wang Zhu was commissioned to arrange them in order and have them engraved into jujube wood blocks within the Secret Pavilion. Consequently, these prints occasionally exhibit **silver ingot** patterns <note>referring to the shape of the joints or repairs in the woodblocks</note>. Shen Meng, in his *Record of the Mulan Embankment in Putian County*, notes that according to local elders, the foundation of the embankment sits upon stone outcroppings at the riverbed which stretch across to the northern mountains. Wherever two stones were joined, a socket was carved in the shape of a **silver ingot**, and molten iron was poured into these joints. This is why the structure can withstand the powerful currents; its durability over time is well-founded. Feng Daosheng, in his *Rhapsody on the Studio of True Appreciation*, mentions the ancient color of Tinggui ink and the **silver ingot** patterns found in jujube wood. Mao <unclear>Weishu</unclear> <note>refers to the Book of Wei</note> states that Cui Hao specialized in <unclear>text missing</unclear>.

Silver Thread <note>original: "銀絲" (Yín Sī)</note>
Du Fu, in his poem *Visiting General He's Mountain Forest*, writes of fresh **silver threads** <note>referring to thin white noodles or shredded vegetables</note> gifted for a soup of fragrant celery and green mountain herbs.

Silver Embroidery <note>original: "銀縷" (Yín Lǚ)</note>
The *History of Song: Treatise on Chariots and Apparel* describes the construction of the Xiezhi Crown <note>a crown featuring a mythical creature symbolizing justice</note>. It was made with bamboo for the frame, wrapped in crimson silk, and used **silver embroidery** for the fine details. A leaf of <unclear>text missing</unclear> was inserted at the back of the crown. Bao Rong, in his poem *Gift for One Traveling Far*, writes that the mud-dance tiger spirit is hidden, and the **silver embroidery** of the crossing dragons appears cold. Yu Ji, in his poem *Song for Zhang Zhonghua’s Promotion and Return South to His Old Post*, offers this for the joy of a smile; the poem can be found under the entry for Jade Nectar.

<keywords>silver ingot, woodblock printing, Mulan Embankment, Du Fu, Song Dynasty apparel, silver thread, calligraphy preservation</keywords>

Silver Basin

Records of Inquiring after the Strange: When Lu Guimeng resided in Wu, an inner official passed through Changzhou. By the water's edge, he saw a flower-duck and shot it dead with a pellet. The caretaker informed Lu Guimeng, who then took a small boat and prepared a formal petition to inform the official, saying: "I was raising this duck, and it was able to speak human language. I was just about to present it to the Emperor. Why did you kill it?" He then showed him the petition. The official was shocked and ashamed, and compensated him with a <term>Silver Basin</term> <gloss>Yin ang</gloss>. Before departing, the official asked what the duck could actually say. Lu replied: "I taught it for several years, and it could call out its own name."

# Iron Fortress <note>Chinese: Tiezhai</note>

The Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Ming Dynasty <note>Ming Yitong Zhi</note> states: Tongguan and the **Iron Fortress** Mountain are located southwest of the Tanxi Chiefdom in Liping Prefecture. The mountain is high and steep, but the summit is quite flat and wide, capable of holding a thousand people. It is protected by natural hazards on three sides, and can only be ascended from the south.

# Iron Market <note>Chinese: Tieshi</note>

The Book of Han, Table of Official Posts and Ceremonies <note>Hanshu Baiguan Gongqing Biao</note> records: The Superintendent of Grain and Agriculture had subordinate officials, including five Directors and Assistants for the Grand Granary, Balanced Transportation, Price Stabilization, the Treasury, and the Imperial Field. There were also two Directors and Assistants for the **Iron Market**. <note>original: Tieshi liang zhangcheng</note>

Xu Ling, Inscription for the Food for the Monks of Changgan Temple <note>Changgan Si Zhongshi Bei</note>: Outside the temple is the **Iron Market** and Copper Street, the brothels and purple paths, the neighborhoods of the Xin family and various clans, and the gates of the noble palaces. There is no one who does not compete in high offerings, and the accumulated supplies grow increasingly numerous.

Yu Xin, Epitaph for Lady Wushilan, Wife of the Duke and General of the Zhou Dynasty: The old city of Fufung still remains, and the **Iron Market** and the old villas of Henan still linger, like the Golden Valley Garden.

# Iron Bridge <note>Chinese: Tieqiao</note>

The Old Book of Tang, Account of Tibet <note>Tangshu Tubo Zhuan</note>: At that time, Wei Gao achieved the greatest merit. He destroyed over fifty fortresses and defeated the Southern Route Marshals Lun Mangre, Meilongqi, and Xinülu. He also joined forces with Nanzhao to defeat them at Shenchuan and at the **Iron Bridge**. Wei Gao captured and beheaded thirty thousand enemies, and accepted the surrender of leaders such as Lun Qiran, Tang Mozang, and Xinülu.

Cao Tang, Poem on Sending the Daoist Wang Xi Back to Mount Luofu: The stone steps lean against the sky, walking with the moon; the **Iron Bridge** leads to the sea, entering without dust.

Su Shi, Poem Following the Rhymes of Elder Qin of Dinghui: The **Iron Bridge** originally has no pillars; how can the Stone Mansion have a door?

Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices <term>Taichang Gong</term> <gloss>the honorable official of ancestral rites and ceremonial protocol</gloss> had just passed the imperial examinations <note>original: "登科"</note>, while all the others were just beginning their studies. Day and night, the sounds of their recitation echoed back and forth. I thought to myself: this is like a mighty tree in the return of spring, its buds and blossoms clustering thickly, blossoming and bearing fruit in great abundance. Who could possibly resist it? Later, everything turned out precisely as expected. Whenever I silently reflected on where their family tradition originated, I never failed to sigh and sing praises repeatedly for the gentleman.

Suddenly, one day, news of his death arrived. I was already grieving deeply for him when his orphaned son sent an intermediary to travel to me and request an epitaph <note>original: "銘"</note>. My grief deepened further, and I said: "How can I bear to write an epitaph for the gentleman? Yet knowing him so deeply, I cannot refuse."

The gentleman's taboo name <note>the formal personal name avoided out of respect</note> was Yiyuan, and his courtesy name was Jiliang. His great-grandfather was named [omitted], his grandfather was named [omitted], and his father was named [omitted], who was appointed by the District School Instructor <term>Xueyu</term> <gloss>an official overseeing local Confucian studies and schools</gloss> to be his heir. When the gentleman was barely fifteen years of age, he conducted his father's funeral rites. His grief and emaciation were as profound as if mourning his own birth father. In managing the burial grounds and family tombs, even those seasoned in worldly affairs could not equal him. He served his mother with celebrated filial devotion. His mother had only two daughters whom she cherished dearly, and the gentleman provided them both with their full inheritance shares when they married.

<summary>Huang Zhen recalls the flourishing scholarly atmosphere of the Sun family school, mourns the death of Sun Yiyuan (Jiliang), and agrees to compose his epitaph, recounting his filial conduct and dutiful family management from youth.</summary>
<keywords>Huang Zhen, Sun Yiyuan, Jiliang, Taichang Gong, imperial examinations, epitaph, funeral rites, filial piety, family inheritance, Xueyu</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>in the township, and the township residents relied upon him for their very survival. In my heart I admired him greatly and intended to record his deeds, but had not yet found the leisure to do so. In the spring of the following year, the Prefectural Professor <term>Jiaoshou</term> <gloss>prefectural education official</gloss> was departing to assume his official post, and he visited me to say farewell. Suddenly he brought out a subterranean tomb record <term>kuangji</term> <gloss>biographical stone tablet placed inside a burial vault</gloss> composed by Academician of the Xianwen Pavilion <note>court title</note> Master Zhao Ruji <note>Song dynasty official and scholar</note> for the Court Gentleman for Consultation <term>Chaofeng</term> <gloss>honorific court title</gloss>, and requested that I compose a tomb inscription <term>muming</term> <gloss>funerary biographical inscription carved on stone</gloss>. I replied that a tomb inscription was originally not something I would dare to presume to write. Yet, if it served to bring forward the recompense of accumulated virtue to encourage others, then this was precisely the duty of one who governs the people, and it could not be left unrecorded. I therefore took Master Zhao's record and examined it. The Court Gentleman for Consultation was by nature exceedingly filial. He once cut flesh from his own thigh <term>duogu</term> <gloss>cutting thigh flesh to brew medicinal broth for an ailing parent, an extreme act of filial devotion</gloss> to heal his mother's illness. He once divined an auspicious site for a dwelling, but instead used it to bury his father, declaring: "Better that I have no home, than that my father lack an auspicious resting place." When neighbors in the village had lawsuits or disputes, he reasoned with them using principle, and the disputes immediately ceased. When someone encountered an evil spirit and fell prostrate upon the road, he lifted their ears and called out to them, and they immediately revived. Such deeds of filial piety and fraternal respect were not only revered by human beings, but were revered even by the ghosts and spirits.

<summary>Huang Zhen recounts how Gentleman Zhang's son presented a vault record by Zhao Ruji and requested a funerary inscription, which Huang accepted as a duty to encourage virtue. Zhao's record reveals Zhang's extraordinary filial piety, including cutting his own thigh flesh to cure his mother, dedicating an auspicious site to his father's grave, and commanding reverence from neighbors and spirits alike.</summary>
<keywords>Huang Zhen, Zhang, Jiaoshou, Zhao Ruji, Chaofeng, kuangji, muming, filial piety, duogu, burial divination, dispute resolution, spirits</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>at Wumen <note>Suzhou</note>. We conversed into the middle of the night. The gentleman spoke copiously of ancient and modern times, analyzing moral principles as if a torrential river could not be checked. I knew that his learning surely came from a profound heritage, though I was not yet able to learn all the details.

From then on, whenever I met scholars from Min <note>Fujian</note>, I invariably inquired about the gentleman's family background. All said that he was the son of Master Aiyin. Master Aiyin possessed ancient learning and an ancient heart, rising aloft and detached without associating with worldly affairs. The gentleman also diligently maintained his late father's ideals; on account of this, he remained unappreciated and thwarted in the world. Because of this, I respected and admired him all the more.

Ten years later, I returned from Jiangxi. The gentleman happened to be serving on the staff of the Coastal Control Commission, and thus I was able to inquire into the detailed life of Master Aiyin. The gentleman looked sorrowful and said: "I have wandered long in official service, and my late father's tomb has not yet been inscribed. I was just wishing to entrust this task to you." I declined, pleading incompetence, two and three times. The next day, he brought his father's biographical account, and I again declined repeatedly, but could not obtain his permission to withdraw. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>Yet the Lady endured poverty alone and swore herself to faithfulness unto death for fifty-five years. How great was her integrity! There are indeed women who do not remarry, yet when the Lady's husband could not attain official rank, she could not bear to remarry someone who held office. How great was her discernment! It is only natural for a mother to hope for her son to attain nobility, yet the Lady was displeased when her son advanced through alternative paths, insisting that he advance through Confucian learning. How great, again, was her aspiration! All of these qualities deserve an inscription, so how could we permit them to go uninscribed? The inscription reads:

In the prime of youth she dwelt in widowhood, her conduct pure as ice and snow;
She instructed her son in the Odes and Documents, her resolve firm as metal and iron.
Alas! Was she not truly the daughter of an illustrious father?
She came near indeed to heroic perfection!

### Epitaph of Sun Chengjie

Jade leaves scatter autumn shadows, the golden wind flutters.
<note>Reference to the changing seasons and the movement of the wind.</note>

Li Bai, in his poem *Gazing at the Waterfall at Mount Lu*: The sun shines on Incense Burner Peak, generating <term>purple smoke</term> <gloss>a misty haze appearing purple in the sunlight</gloss>. Looking from afar, the waterfall hangs before the river.
<note>Li Bai is one of China’s most famous Tang dynasty poets; this is one of his most celebrated landscape poems.</note>

Yan Deyin, in the poem *Song of the Flower Candles for Prince Xue*: One should only hope to quickly acquire the arts of Huainan <note>referring to alchemy or immortality</note>, then one will see the <term>beast smoke</term> <gloss>smoke from animal-shaped incense burners</gloss> fly into the <term>cloud smoke</term>.

*Book of Liang*, Biography of Zhang Hongce: He constantly followed the High Ancestor <note>Emperor Wu of Liang</note> in his travels and dwellings. Every time he entered the room, he always sensed a <term>cloudy smoke-like vapor</term> <gloss>an auspicious aura or spiritual energy</gloss>; his body would immediately become solemn. Because of this, he especially revered the High Ancestor.

Lu Ji, in a poem: Autumn grass overflows the long branches, cold water enters the <term>cloud smoke</term>.

Xie Lingyun, in a poem: Then climbing to the head of the various peaks, appearing distant as if ascending into the <term>cloud smoke</term>.
<note>Xie Lingyun was a pioneer of Chinese landscape poetry.</note>

Song Zhiwen, in the poem *Climbing the Pavilion of Chanding Temple*: Opening my robe, I sit amidst the high heavens; waving my hand, I brush away the <term>cloud smoke</term>.

Du Fu, in the *Song of the Eight Immortals of the Winecup*: Zhang Xu, after three cups, is the master of cursive script; waving his brush, it falls on the paper, surpassing the <term>cloud smoke</term>.
<note>Zhang Xu was a famous Tang calligrapher known for his wild cursive style.</note>

*Book of Tang*, Annals of Taizong: In the seventeenth year of the Zhenguan era, in the second month, portraits of the meritorious officials were painted in the <term>Lingyan Pavilion</term> <gloss>literally "Pavilion Surpassing the Smoke"</gloss>. 

Also, the Annals of Daizong: In the first year of the Guangde era, iron certificates were given to meritorious officials and stored in the Imperial Ancestral Temple; their likenesses were painted in the <term>Lingyan Pavilion</term>. 

Du Fu, in *An Introduction to Painting*: The meritorious officials in the <term>Lingyan Pavilion</term> have faded in color; the General <note>referring to the painter Cao Ba</note> puts down his brush and gives them new life.

Also, a poem by Yu Shinan: Two white cranes come flying, spreading their wings to travel far into the <term>cloud smoke</term> <note>original: "Lingyan"</note>.

<term>Lingyan</term> <gloss>Surpassing the Smoke</gloss> is also written as <term>Lingyan</term> <gloss>Ascending the Smoke</gloss>. *Biographies of the Immortals*: Ningzi entered the fire and ascended into the smoke.

*Master Yan*: A five-foot child <unclear>three</unclear> inches of <unclear>cloud smoke</unclear>. The whole world cannot be sufficient to <unclear>...</unclear>

New <unclear>...</unclear> taboo name Long <unclear>...</unclear> Yu Mo Long <unclear>...</unclear> Behead. Now those surrounding you are all <unclear>cloud smoke</unclear> followers, yet you ultimately do not know it.

Sparse Emerald Leaves
<note>Reference to a poetic description of foliage.</note>
As the rain passes, the red garments <note>petals</note> fall. Song Wushuang’s Backgammon poem: The golden threads mark the mulberry grain where the game ended; firm red clouds dip into the water.
<column-break/>
The vast sea of the Treasury of Wisdom Sutra <note>original: "智藏經" (Zhizhang Jing)</note>: Like the flower in the autumn moon, it is something all people delight to see.
Mountain Lotus
Li Qiao’s poem: Looking back, I recognize the trees of Pingling; looking down, I see the mountain lotus.
Du Fu’s poem: The clouds break above the great road.
The sky clears and the palace willows darken in the Eternal Spring. Zhang Bin’s poem on the solitary pine of Mount Hua: Its roots draw from the stone crevices, not from the strength of the soil; braving the cold, it still assists the autumn lotus.
Li Bai’s Music Bureau poem: Falling stars and white feathers tucked at the waist; the sword flower’s <note>the pattern or glint of the blade</note> light emerges from the scabbard. Meng Jiao’s poem: Scriptural texts open upon cowry leaves; garments are fashioned with hanging lotus.
Wei Zhuang’s poem on the East Lake of the Three Halls: The toad <note>the moon</note> casts its nocturnal soul as it falls into the lake; the mountain lotus falls.
Love for the Lotus
Master Zhou <note>Zhou Dunyi</note>’s treatise: I alone love the lotus for emerging from the mud yet remaining unstained, for being washed by clear ripples yet not appearing seductive. It stands tall and pure, planted upright; it can be viewed from a distance but not handled profanely. It is the gentleman among flowers.
Face-like Lotus
Ouyang Xiu’s poem: The lamp flower plays upon the powdered colors; the wine’s redness rises in the lotus-like face.
Lotus in a Bowl
The Book of Jin, Biography of Fotudeng: Shi Le summoned Fotudeng to test his spiritual arts. Deng took a bowl filled with water, and in a moment, a blue lotus flower grew within it, its colors radiant and shining.
Joined-Joy Lotus <note>original: "合懽蓮" (Hehuan Lian), referring to two lotus flowers sharing a single stem</note>
History of Song: In the ninth year of the Xingguo era, a pot of auspicious lotuses from the Yujin Garden was shown to the ministers; the flowers and leaves were all joined in joy as they grew. Liu Zongyuan’s memorial: I humbly observe that this month, the blue lotus from the Dingli Pond in the Western Palace and the joined-joy lotus from before the Shenlong Temple were shown to the officials.
Prime Minister’s Lotus
Supplement to the National History: The Minister of State, Yu Di, thought the name of the musical piece "Thinking of My Husband" <note>original: "想夫憐" (Xiang Fu Lian)</note> was not elegant and wished to change it. A guest said: In the Southern Dynasties, there was an auspicious lotus in the Prime Minister’s residence, thus it was called the "Prime Minister’s Lotus" <note>original: "相府蓮" (Xiang Fu Lian)</note>. Since then, people’s speech became corrupted, and the error was passed down.

<meta>The text is from the Peiwen Yunfu, a Qing dynasty encyclopedia of literary phrases and rhymes. This section covers terms related to agriculture and fields.</meta>

# Imperial Edition of the Peiwen Yunfu: Volume 16, Part 3

Can be made one by one <note>referring to the layout of fields</note>. Three furrows per year are rotated, therefore it is called an ancient method. Houji <note>the legendary Lord of Millet, patron of agriculture</note> first began the furrowed field system. Using two plows as a pair, a space one foot wide and one foot deep is called a <term>quan</term> <gloss>furrow</gloss>. The length reaches the end of the plot. One <term>mu</term> <gloss>unit of land area</gloss> contains three furrows. One laborer manages three hundred furrows. The commentary states that furrows are the ridges between fields. They are rotated and exchanged.

### Furrowed Fields
<term>Quan tian</term> <gloss>Furrowed fields</gloss>. See above.

### Diligent Farming
<term>Li tian</term> <gloss>Diligent farming</gloss>. The Book of Han, Annals of Emperor Hui, states that those among the people who are filial, brotherly, and <unclear>diligent in farming</unclear> shall be exempt from labor service. Also, in the Annals of Emperor Wen, it states that the positions of the Three Elders, the Filial, the Brotherly, and the <unclear>diligent farmers</unclear> were established as permanent staff. Further, an imperial decree stated that filial piety and fraternal duty are the great virtues of the world, and <unclear>diligent farming</unclear> is the foundation of life. In the History of the Northern Dynasties, Biography of Yan Yuanming, it is recorded that he supported his mother with notable filial piety in his village, and through <unclear>diligent farming</unclear>, he accumulated grain and gave it away to others without ceasing. Du Fu, in his writings on the East and West Sichuan regions, mentioned that displaced people drifting through various prefectures and counties are only serving the interests of powerful families through <unclear>diligent farming</unclear>.

### Sacred Field
<term>Ji tian</term> <gloss>Sacred field or plowing field</gloss>. The Book of Han, Annals of Emperor Wen, contains a decree stating that agriculture is the foundation of the world. Therefore, the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear> should be opened, and I, the Emperor, will personally lead the plowing to provide the grain offerings for the ancestral temples. Ying Shao's commentary notes that <term>ji</term> refers to the constant records and rituals of emperors and kings. Wei Zhao's commentary notes that <term>ji</term> means to borrow, specifically borrowing the labor of the people to manage it. Furthermore, the Table of Official Ranks states that the Grand Minister of Agriculture has a subordinate official called the Director of the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear>. The Old Book of Tang, Treatise on Ritual and Music, mentions that in the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear>, sacrifices are made to the First Farmer. In the early Tang, this was also the Altar of the Imperial Earth, also called the Altar of the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear>. In the Biography of Cen Wenben, it is noted that in the first year of the Zhenguan era, after Emperor Taizong had performed the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear> ritual and met with the officials, Cen Wenben presented two odes on the <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear> and the Three Primaries. The writing was elegant and ornate. The Springs and Autumns of Master Lü states that in the first month of spring, the Son of Heaven leads the Three Ducal Ministers, the Nine Ministers, the Feudal Lords, and the Grandees to personally plow the Imperial <unclear>Sacred Field</unclear>.

### Military Colony
<term>Tun tian</term> <gloss>Military agricultural colony</gloss>. The Book of Han, Annals of Emperor Zhao, states that in the autumn of the second year, former officials were transferred to lead the <unclear>military colonies</unclear> in Zhangye Commandery. In the Biography of Zhao Chongguo, it says that maintaining the <unclear>military colonies</unclear> yielded twelve advantages, while withdrawing the troops would result in twelve losses. In the Que Sao Bian, it is mentioned that Liu Yong became famous for his song lyrics during the reign of Emperor Renzong. He served as the Vice Director of <unclear>Military Colonies</unclear>, hence the world called him Liu <unclear>Tun-tian</unclear>. The Record of Transmitting Information from Yichun states that the Director of <unclear>Military Colonies</unclear>, Mr. Li Quming, served as the Vice Prefect of Junzhou during the Mingdao era. Former officials received the autumn tax from the clerks.

Returning to the Field <note>original: 復田</note>
The Book of Changes Oracle <note>original: 易林</note> says: When a scholar becomes an official, he does not lose his meals. It is like <term>returning to the field</term> <gloss>returning to farming</gloss> to gain long life and preserve one's years.

Marshes and Fields <note>original: 臯田</note>
The Book of Changes Oracle <note>original: 易林</note> says: In the <term>marshes and fields</term>, the grain and millet are piled high like soil, and the hemp grows in abundance.

Ceasing the Hunt <note>original: 罷田</note>
The Garden of Stories <note>original: 說苑</note> records: King Zhuang of Chu loved hunting. When his ministers remonstrated with him, the King replied: I hunt in order to seek out talented men. Those who face the thickets to stab tigers and leopards, I know to be brave. Those who seize rhinoceroses and fight wild bulls, I know to be strong and powerful. When we <term>cease the hunt</term> and divide the catch, I know who is benevolent. By this way, I obtained three worthy men, and thus the State of Chu was at peace.

Old Fields <note>original: 舊田</note>
The New Preface <note>original: 新序</note> records: Duke Wen of Jin taxed <term>old fields</term> at half the rate, while new fields were not taxed at all.

Jade Fields <note>original: 瓊田</note>
The Records of the Ten Islands <note>original: 十洲記</note> states: On Ancestor Island <note>original: 祖洲</note> grows the herb of immortality, which grows within <term>jade fields</term>. It is sometimes called the "Spirit-Nourishing Mushroom." Its leaves resemble wild rice and grow in clusters; a single stalk can revive a person. Zhang Zhengjian wrote in a poem on snow: At Suiyang, jade trees are born; at Yunmeng, <term>jade fields</term> arise. Yu Xin wrote in his letter of thanks to the King of Zhao for gifts of silk and cloth: The sleet is like <term>jade fields</term>, and the ice is like the salt banks. Gu Kuang wrote in his Song of the Higher Purity: In <term>jade fields</term> the immortal grass lives forever. Ouyang Xiu wrote in his poem on the Canglang Pavilion: When the wind is high and the moon white, it is most suitable at night; a single stretch of pure luster spreads across the <term>jade fields</term>. Zhu Xi wrote in his poem on celery: When will the <term>jade fields</term> be planted? The jade roots are born all at once.

Altar Fields <note>original: 壇田</note>
The Rituals of the Han Officials <note>original: 漢官儀</note> states: The Emperor has <term>altar fields</term>. After the high officials finish plowing, the agricultural officer sows the seeds.

Prioritizing Fields <note>original: 先田</note>
The Balanced Discourses <note>original: 論衡</note> states: A man having a house is like having a field. One uses the field for food and drink, and the house for living. Among the things people value, food is the most urgent. Therefore, one <term>prioritizes the fields</term> and places the house second, as fields are more important than houses.

Stony Fields <note>original: 宕田</note>
The Records of Hanzhong <note>original: 漢中志</note> states: In Fu County, the waters connect to Ba; there are <term>stony fields</term> and flat rice fields.

Luo Fields <note>original: 雒田</note>
The Commentary on the Water Classic <note>original: 水經注</note> states: In Jiaozhi <note>Annam/Northern Vietnam</note>, before there were commanderies or counties, the land had <term>Luo fields</term>. These fields followed the rise and fall of the tide. The people who cleared and ate from these fields were thus named the Luo people.

Improper or unclean; a minor transgression. Regarding the person of the highest honor, <note>the Emperor</note>, committing a minor transgression <note>original: 小過</note> is not appropriate for one of such status.

### Frequent Punishment
In the *Book of the Heart* <note>original: 心書</note> it says: One who rewards frequently is in distress; one who gives **frequent punishment** <note>original: 屢罰</note> is in difficulty.

### Manifest Punishment
In the *New Treatise* <note>original: 新論</note> by Liu Xie: Clearly rewarding the virtuous is the means to encourage good people. **Manifest punishment** <note>original: 顯罰</note> for those who have transgressed is the means to prohibit villainy among the subordinates.

### Single Punishment
In the *New Treatise* by Liu Xie: A single reward cannot be given without being trusted; a **single punishment** <note>original: 一罰</note> cannot be administered without being clear.

### Encountering Punishment
In the *Songs of Chu* <note>original: 楚辭</note>, section on Loyalty: What crime have I committed to **encounter punishment** <note>original: 遇罰</note>? This was truly not my intention.

### Severe Punishment
In the *Discourse on Government* <note>original: 政論</note> by Cui Shi: Now, since we cannot purely follow the methods of the ancient world, we should incorporate elements of the Hegemon’s rule. We should use heavy rewards and **severe punishment** <note>original: 深罰</note> to govern them, and clearly manifest laws and political arts to examine them.

### Inviting Punishment
In the *Treatise on Nourishing Life* <note>original: 攝生論</note> by Xi Kang: One must accumulate goodness before a blessing responds; trust must be established before protection arrives. This is like a crime **inviting punishment** <note>original: 招罰</note> or merit resulting in reward. In Fu Xian’s *Letter in Reply to Yang Ji*: To defy the orders of superiors or cause delays is to **invite punishment**.

### Accumulated Punishment
In the *Discourse on Interpreting the Times* <note>original: 釋時論</note> by Wang Chen: If a man’s character is thin but his position is high, his **accumulated punishment** <note>original: 積罰</note> will make the responsibility difficult to bear.

### Drinking-Cup Punishment
In a poem by Wei Yingwu: Letting the spirit go and leaving behind what constrains it; the **drinking-cup punishment** <note>original: 觥罰</note> is frequently seen during the exchange of toasts <note>note: a penalty involving drinking wine during a game or banquet</note>.

### Kindness and Punishment
In Han Yu’s *Prayer to the Spirits of the Bamboo Grove*: The spirits make no error in their distribution of **kindness and punishment** <note>original: 惠罰</note>. If the punishment for my sins falls upon the body of me, Han Yu, making me thin and ill, I shall find it sweet and appropriate.

### Arbitrary Punishment
In the *Policy Documents* by Li Xuancheng: Since the Way is distant and the Sages have passed, extravagance reached the Qin and Liu-Song dynasties. They offered silks to stir up profit, and viewed gold as a means for **arbitrary punishment** <note>original: 逞罰</note>.

### Calling for Punishment
In a poem by Huang Tao: With every word, the horses ride together to visit the prominent families; a thousand types of **calling for punishment** <note>original: 唱罰</note> or rewards happen within the Imperial Capital.

### Comparison to Punishment
In the *Book of Documents* <note>original: 書經</note>: I have supported you and caused you to be happy and healthy. If you are not respectful, you will have faults which will be **compared to punishment** <note>original: 比于罰</note>.

### Punishment from Above
In the *Book of Documents*: The former sovereigns will send down great suffering and illness upon you, saying, "Why did you not support our young grandson?" Because you have strayed in virtue, there is **punishment from above** <note>original: 自上罰</note>.

<keywords>punishment, justice, legalism, Liu Xie, Cui Shi, Book of Documents, Songs of Chu, classical Chinese law, rewards and punishments</keywords>

Departed and ultimately no one knew where he had gone.

### Soldiers of Shu
<note>original: 蜀卒</note>
History of the Five Dynasties, Biography of Wang Huan: When Emperor Shizong <note>Chai Rong, second emperor of the Later Zhou</note> campaigned against the Huai region for the second time, he sent Wang Huan to lead several thousand <term>Soldiers of Shu</term> in naval warfare, entering the Huai River via the Cai River. While Huan was in the army, he never achieved any military merit. The <term>Soldiers of Shu</term> who were captured along with Huan were not killed by Shizong, but were all drafted into his own military service.

### Accumulated Soldiers
<note>original: 積卒</note>
History of the Song Dynasty, Treatise on Astronomy: The <term>Accumulated Soldiers</term> are twelve stars located southwest of the Fang <note>Room</note> constellation; they represent the imagery of five military camps. The Classic of Stars states: Below the front of the Fang constellation, the twelve stars of the <term>Accumulated Soldiers</term> are located southeast of the Di <note>Root</note> constellation; these stars are faint and small.

### Laboring Soldiers
<note>original: 工卒</note>
History of the Song Dynasty, Treatise on Food and Money: Since the Bian River boats did not reach the lands beyond the Yangtze, and the boats from beyond the Yangtze could not reach the capital, the profits of merchant trade were lost. When the <term>Laboring Soldiers</term> of the Bian boats finished their work, they each sat and ate their rations, constantly suffering from insufficiency.

### Transport Soldiers
<note>original: 漕卒</note>
History of the Song Dynasty, Treatise on Food and Money: In the fifth year of the Jiayou era <note>1060 AD</note>, commentators initially wanted the <term>Transport Soldiers</term> to be able to return home to rest. However, many Bian boats hired laborers, and each boat had no more than one or two actual soldiers. When winter came and they had to stay to guard the boats, in reality, none of them were able to return home to rest.

### Stable Soldiers
<note>original: 廐卒</note>
History of the Song Dynasty, Treatise on Food and Money: In the fifth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era <note>1012 AD</note>, Duan Weiji dispatched two hundred laborers from Zhongmu County to repair the Imperial Horse Bureau granaries. The Supervisory Commissioner replaced them with <term>Stable Soldiers</term>, whereupon an imperial edict was issued to forbid this practice.

### Regard the Soldiers
<note>original: 視卒</note>
The Classic of the Hidden Accord <note>original: Yin Fu Jing</note>.
Sun Wu <note>Sun Tzu</note> said: If you <term>Regard the Soldiers</term> as your beloved sons, they can die with you. If you <term>Regard the Soldiers</term> as infants, they can go with you into deep valleys.

### Human Soldiers
<note>original: 人卒</note>
Zhuangzi: Although Heaven and Earth are great, their transformation is uniform. Although the myriad things are numerous, their governance is one. Although <term>Human Soldiers</term> are many, their master is the Ruler.
Han Yu, Stele on the Pacification of Huaixi: Li Su set out from Wencheng. Taking advantage of a great snowstorm, he galloped swiftly and reached Caizhou at midnight. He captured Wu Yuanji to present him to the Emperor, and seized all his subordinates and <term>Human Soldiers</term>.

### Formed Soldiers
<note>original: 成卒</note>
Xunzi: When the troops of a benevolent man gather, they act as <term>Formed Soldiers</term>; when they disperse, they form orderly ranks.

### Official Soldiers
<note>original: 官卒</note>
Han Fei Zi: When Guo Yan first began to govern, Duke Wen of Jin provided him with <term>Official Soldiers</term>.

### Trained Soldiers
<note>original: 練卒</note>
Lüshi Chunqiu: When Zhang Zi attacked the State of Jing <note>Chu</note>, he sent men to observe the water to see where it could be crossed. There was a man from Shu by the water who said: The shallow and deep parts of the water are easy to know. The people of Jing...

<keywords>Wang Huan, Five Dynasties, Song Dynasty history, Astronomy, Sun Tzu, Han Yu, military labor, transportation, logistics</keywords>

Pursuing the Way across rivers and lakes with wealth and treasures, he arrived at Wumen <note>modern Suzhou</note>. Knowing that Zhou Yinyao had left the world to practice cultivation, he went directly to Mount Dongting to visit him. He brought gold and silk to fund the incense and candles. He’s dream of thirst was suddenly fulfilled in the vast waters; not even a tiny drop remained <term>unsoaked</term> <gloss>un-absorbed or not moistened</gloss>.
### Dried Up
The History of the Southern Dynasties, Biography of Sun Fazong: Fazong's father followed Sun En into the seaside and was killed, but his remains were not recovered. Fazong went into the sea to search for them. He heard a worldly saying that if one is a close relative, their blood will soak into the bones <note>a traditional belief used to identify kinship</note>. He took a knife and went along the coast; whenever he saw withered bones, he cut his flesh to pour blood upon them. He did this for over ten years until there was no whole skin left on his arms or legs and his blood vessels were <term>completely exhausted</term>. In the end, he could not find the remains and wore mourning clothes for the rest of his life. The Philosophical Disputations <note>Lunheng</note>: The waters of the rivers and streams surge and leak away; flowing across the vast earth, there is no stream that is <term>dried up</term>.
### Source Abundance
### Arrows Exhausted
The History of the Chen Dynasty, Biography of Wu Mingche: Like Li Ling whose <term>arrows were exhausted</term>, he could not avoid surrendering to Yu Jin. Even though the waters rose, he was captured alive. Note: Li Ling's Letter to Su Wu writes this as "arrows depleted."
### Labor Exhausted
History of the Northern Dynasties, Annals of Emperor Gaozu of Sui: His physical strength and spirit were <term>temporarily exhausted</term>. Zhuangzi: If the spirit is used without ceasing, it becomes labored; if labored, it is <term>fully exhausted</term>.
The History of Tang, Biography of Zhang Xun: When the rebels attacked the city, the soldiers were ill and could not fight. Xun bowed toward the West and said: "This isolated city cannot be preserved. Your servant cannot repay Your Majesty in life; I shall become a ghost in death to strike the rebels."
### State Exhausted
History of the Five Dynasties, Biographies of Zhou Officials, Wang Pu: When Shizong ascended the throne, Pu was promoted to Bureau Director in the Ministry of Justice and presented a strategy for pacifying the borders. He said: "The way of conquest begins with what is easy. Currently, only the Wu region is easy to plot against. We should harass them with light troops. They will surely mobilize in great numbers to respond. Repeated mobilizations will distress the people and the <term>state will be exhausted</term>. If they do not mobilize, we gain the advantage. When they are exhausted and we have the advantage, the prefectures north of the Yangtze River will belong to our nation."
### Siege Exhaustion
The Lost Book of Zhou, Kaiwang chapter: If the land is broad but undefended, it can be raided. If the land is narrow and lacks food, it will suffer <term>exhaustion under siege</term>. These two calamities are disasters of disproportion.
### Left Exhausted
The Lost Book of Zhou: Much land but few people.

<summary>This page catalogs historical and literary usages of terms related to exhaustion and depletion, specifically regarding physical strength, military resources, and state finances. It includes anecdotes of filial piety and strategic military counsel from the Southern Dynasties through the Five Dynasties period.</summary>
<keywords>Sun Fazong, blood on bones, Li Ling, Zhang Xun, Wang Pu, military strategy, filial piety, Lost Book of Zhou, linguistics, historical records</keywords>

<meta>The text contains excerpts from the Imperial Parallel Characters (Pianzi Leibian), an encyclopedic dictionary of literary phrases. This section focuses on phrases related to geographical locations, specifically involving the character Xiang (referring to the Xiang River region or Hunan) and Hubei.</meta>

# Volume 53

<note>The following entries discuss the administrative history and literary mentions of the Xiang River region.</note>

The Provincial Government was located in Ezhou but was moved to the **Xiang River** <note>The original text uses a placeholder 丨丨 to represent the headword Xiang-jiang</note> Circuit; the Pacification Commission was governed from Tanzhou. In the second year of the Tianli era <note>1329 CE</note>, because it was the favored residence of the Emperor before his accession, it was renamed Tianlin Circuit. 

Han Yu, in his *Preface for the Departure of He Jian*: Jian is a man of Daozhou. The Governor of Dao, Master Yang, is a man of virtue. Daozhou is a subordinate prefecture within the **Xiang River** region. The Governor of the **Xiang River** region, Master Yang <note>referring to Yang Jingshi</note>, is also a man of virtue. Jian is a commoner, and Jian is also a man of virtue. The **Xiang River** region gained Daozhou as its subordinate; Daozhou gained Jian as its citizen. When Jian returns, he will lead the elders and youth of his prefecture to obey Master Yang’s commands; Daozhou will also lead its counties and neighboring prefectures to obey Master Yang’s commands. 

Li Jiayou, in his poem *Sending off Administrator Yan*: Seen above and below the **Xiang River**. 

Yuan Zhen, in his poem *Sending off Wang Eleven on his Journey South*: Ten thousand miles beneath the **Xiang River** moon; three cries of the apes upon the mountains. 

Jiaoran, in his poem *Thoughts of Yan Shihe while Traveling by Boat*: In the second month, the **Xiang River** spring grass spreads everywhere; at the Hengshan ferry, flowers fall like sleet. 

Yang Weizhen, in his poem *Sending off Fei Mengchen North and for the Attention of the Eighteenth Gentleman*: I ask you, man of **Xiang River** fame, serving as an envoy; on your green-clothed dapple-gray horse, you truly ride with elegance.

## Hubei

*Book of Qi*, *Biography of Empress Pei*: The imperial carriage frequently visited Langya Castle. The palace attendants always followed, setting out early; by the time they reached the **Hubei** embankment, the roosters would just begin to crow. 

*History of Song*, *Treatise on Food and Money*: In the fifth year of the Huangyou era <note>1053 CE</note>, an imperial edict stated: Recently, **Hubei** suffered a year of scarcity, and the Ever-Normal Granaries were opened to relieve the hungry. We have heard that the Court of Agricultural Affairs is again demanding repayment; how can this be the Court's intention for relief? Let these debts be entirely abolished. 

*History of Yuan*, *Treatise on Official Posts*: The Branch Censorates for the various circuits of Jiangnan had officials of the same rank as the Palace Censorate. In the fourteenth year of the Zhiyuan era <note>1277 CE</note>, the Jiangnan Branch Censorate was first established in Yangzhou; it was soon moved to Hangzhou, then to Jiangzhou. In the twenty-third year <note>1286 CE</note>, it was moved to Jian <note>Jiankang, modern Nanjing</note>.

<summary>This page records historical administrative changes and poetic references concerning the Xiang River region and Hubei province, citing sources from the Tang, Song, and Yuan dynasties.</summary>
<keywords>Xiang River, Hubei, Han Yu, administrative history, Yuan Dynasty, Song Dynasty, classical poetry, famine relief</keywords>

Marsh and Land
<note>the characters Ze Di</note>

The Song of the Hexagrams in the Book of Changes <note>original: Zhou Yi Gua Ge</note> mentions Lake over Earth, which is the Gathering hexagram <note>original: Cui</note>. In the Rites of Zhou <note>original: Zhou Li</note>, the Officer of Rice says that for all crops in the marshes, one should use water in the summer to destroy the weeds and then mow them down. The commentary states that those who intend to use <term>Ze Di</term> <gloss>marshy land</gloss> for crops must wait until the sixth month of summer when the heavy rains fall. This water is used to sicken and cut off any late-growing weeds. By autumn, the water dries up, and the area is mown. The following year, the land can be farmed. Marshes are prone to turning over and becoming soft. The sub-commentary explains that <term>Ze Di</term> <gloss>marshy land</gloss> has much mud and is soft. Master Yuan says that turning over means the mud is sticky and one desires the center <unclear>to be within while the outside is slick</unclear>.

Marsh and Fire
<note>the characters Ze Huo</note>

The Song of the Hexagrams in the Book of Changes <note>refers to the Ge or Revolution hexagram</note>.

Marsh and Field
<note>the characters Ze Ye</note>

The Rites of Zhou, under the Officer of Marshes <note>original: Ze Yu</note>, states that during great hunts, the weeds are cleared from the <term>Ze Ye</term> <gloss>marshy fields</gloss>. When the hunting is finished, the Officer of Marshes plants his banners to gather the captured game.

Marsh and Farmland
<note>the characters Ze Tian</note>

In the Classic of Poetry <note>original: Shi Jing</note>, the section Luxuriant is the Mugwort <note>original: Jing Jing Zhe E</note> says it grows in the middle of the riverbank. Lu Ji's sub-commentary states that the <term>E</term> <gloss>mugwort</gloss> is a type of wormwood. It grows in <term>Ze Tian</term> <gloss>marshy farmland</gloss> and muddy places. Its leaves resemble slant-wormwood but are finer, and the stalks grow in the third month.

Marshy Country
<note>the characters Ze Guo</note>

The History of the Song Dynasty, Treatise on Music <note>original: Song Shi Yue Zhi</note>, says that the upper reaches of the Jing and Chu regions are essential <term>Ze Guo</term> <gloss>marshy country</gloss>, where the Dongting Lake is deep. One recognizes that in this era of unified writing, all hearts turn toward the North Star. Liang Su, in the Preface to Sending Vice-Envoy Cui Back to the Hongzhou Government Office, notes that <term>Ze Guo</term> <gloss>marshy country</gloss> has much rain, and the fragrant flowers are long distressed. Li Deyu, in his Treatise on Retirement <note>original: Tui Shen Lun</note>, writes that when I previously served in the Prime Minister's office and resigned due to illness, I soon sought a distant place in <term>Ze Guo</term> <gloss>marshy country</gloss>. I told myself I would be safe being away from court, not knowing that Heaven is high and does not hear.

<summary>This page catalogs classical literary and ritual references to various terms combining marsh or lake with land, fields, and country. It draws from the Book of Changes, the Rites of Zhou, and Tang dynasty essays to explain agricultural practices and geographical descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>marshland, agriculture, Book of Changes, Rites of Zhou, mugwort, Song Dynasty, Li Deyu</keywords>

<header>Imperially Commissioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries</header>

### Gold <note>The heading indicates the broader category of the entries following</note>

#### Canal Sluices <note>original: 渠竇 qúdòu</note>
In the Book of Tang, Records of the Five Elements: In the second year of the Shangyuan era <note>761 CE</note>, there were continuous autumn rains for months. Fish were born within the **canal sluices**.

#### Canal Embankments <note>original: 渠塘 qútáng</note>
In the History of Song, Biography of Fan Zhongyan: Every year, orders were sent in advance to the various circuits for officials and citizens to report on the benefits and harms concerning agricultural lands. Regarding the dikes, weirs, **canal embankments**, and ponds, the prefectures and counties selected officials to manage them. Laws for encouraging and supervising labor were established to promote agricultural interests and reduce water transport costs. The polder fields of Jiangnan and the river embankments of western Zhejiang that had fallen into ruin could thus be restored.

#### Canal Weirs <note>original: 渠堨 qúè</note>
In the Book of Tang, Biography of Zhang Shougui: An imperial edict designated Gua Prefecture as a Governor-Generalship and appointed Shougui as the Governor-General. The land of the prefecture was sandy and barren, unsuitable for cultivation. They usually stored snow water to irrigate the fields. At that time, the **canal weirs** were destroyed by the barbarians <note>referring to the Khitans or local nomadic forces</note>. There was no timber available to repair them. Shougui prayed secretly to the spirits. One night, the water rose violently, and thousands of large logs blocked the flow and floated down. He took them to repair the weirs and defenses. The farmers returned to their previous work. The people of the prefecture considered it divine and carved an account of the event in stone.

#### Canal Dams <note>original: 渠堰 qúyàn</note>
In the Book of Tang, Records of State Offices: The Directorate of Waterways has two Commissioners. They oversee the administration of rivers, marshes, ferries, bridges, embankments, and ponds.
In the History of Song, Records of Rivers and Canals: The two **canal dams** once irrigated a total of 4,450,000 <term>qing</term> <gloss>a unit of area equal to 100 mu</gloss> of land. Today, less than two-tenths of that remains. Recent repairs have gradually ruined the old defenses. Consequently, the benefits of irrigation are far fewer than in ancient times.
